Assigning a user to a variant needs three properties. The same user must always get the same variant (consistency across page loads). The assignment should not require any round trip (no server call, no cookie write). Variants should distribute evenly by weight even on small samples.

MurmurHash3 handles all three. It is a non-cryptographic hash function designed for lookup keys: fast, well-distributed, and deterministic. The 32-bit version is thirty lines of code and produces a uniform integer from any string input.

export function murmurhash3(key: string, seed: number = 0): number {
  let h1 = seed >>> 0;
  const len = key.length;
  const nblocks = len >> 2;
  const c1 = 0xcc9e2d51;
  const c2 = 0x1b873593;

  for (let i = 0; i < nblocks; i++) {
    let k1 =
      (key.charCodeAt(i * 4) & 0xff) |
      ((key.charCodeAt(i * 4 + 1) & 0xff) << 8) |
      ((key.charCodeAt(i * 4 + 2) & 0xff) << 16) |
      ((key.charCodeAt(i * 4 + 3) & 0xff) << 24);

    k1 = Math.imul(k1, c1);
    k1 = (k1 << 15) | (k1 >>> 17);
    k1 = Math.imul(k1, c2);

    h1 ^= k1;
    h1 = (h1 << 13) | (h1 >>> 19);
    h1 = Math.imul(h1, 5) + 0xe6546b64;
  }

  // tail handling and final mix ...
  return h1 >>> 0;
}

The constants and are the MurmurHash3 mixing multipliers from Austin Appleby's original implementation. They are not magic numbers I made up: they were chosen because they produce good avalanche behaviour, which means flipping a single input bit flips about half the output bits. That property is what gives you even distribution.

matters. JavaScript numbers are 64-bit floats, so naive multiplication of two 32-bit integers can exceed 2^53 and lose precision. performs the multiplication modulo 2^32 with correct sign handling, which is exactly what MurmurHash needs.

Assignment composes the visitor ID and experiment key into the hash input, so the same visitor gets a different variant in each experiment but always the same variant in a single experiment:

export function assignVariant(
  visitorId: string,
  experimentKey: string,
  variants: { key: string; weight: number }[]
): string {
  const hash = murmurhash3(`${visitorId}:${experimentKey}`) % 100;
  let cumulative = 0;
  for (const v of variants) {
    cumulative += v.weight;
    if (hash < cumulative) return v.key;
  }
  return variants[variants.length - 1].key;
}

Weights are percentages summing to 100. Unequal splits (like 90/10 for a gradual rollout) work out of the box. No server call, no cookie, no state. Give the SDK a visitor ID from your own session and it computes the same answer every time.

Statistical significance: two-proportion z-test

The second thing Flip does beyond most DIY A/B stacks is compute significance properly. Showing "variant A got 12% conversion, variant B got 14%" is a presentation failure, not a statistical one: without a p-value, the reader has no way to know whether the difference is signal or noise.

A two-proportion z-test compares two conversion rates and returns the probability of a difference at least this large if the variants really converted at the same rate:

function zTest(
  conversionsA: number, exposuresA: number,
  conversionsB: number, exposuresB: number
): { zScore: number; pValue: number; confidence: number } {
  const pA = exposuresA > 0 ? conversionsA / exposuresA : 0;
  const pB = exposuresB > 0 ? conversionsB / exposuresB : 0;
  const pPooled = (conversionsA + conversionsB) / (exposuresA + exposuresB);

  const se = Math.sqrt(
    pPooled * (1 - pPooled) * (1 / exposuresA + 1 / exposuresB)
  );

  const zScore = (pB - pA) / se;
  const pValue = 2 * (1 - normalCdf(Math.abs(zScore)));
  const confidence = (1 - pValue) * 100;

  return { zScore, pValue, confidence };
}

The pooled proportion is used in the standard error because under the null hypothesis the two variants share a single true conversion rate. Using separate proportions in the SE biases the test. This is the textbook move, and it matters: skipping it is one of the most common DIY A/B bugs.

is two-tailed because you do not know in advance which variant will win. The dashboard shows as a "confidence" percentage for readability, but it is not the probability that the variant is better. "Significant" is defined as , which is just : the standard 5% false-positive rate when there is no real difference.

is the Abramowitz and Stegun polynomial approximation to the standard normal cumulative distribution function. It has six constants and maximum error of about 7.5 × 10⁻⁸, which is more than good enough for A/B results:

function normalCdf(z: number): number {
  const a1 = 0.254829592;
  const a2 = -0.284496736;
  const a3 = 1.421413741;
  const a4 = -1.453152027;
  const a5 = 1.061405429;
  const p = 0.3275911;

  const sign = z < 0 ? -1 : 1;
  z = Math.abs(z) / Math.SQRT2;
  const t = 1.0 / (1.0 + p * z);
  const y = 1.0 - ((((a5 * t + a4) * t + a3) * t + a2) * t + a1) * t * Math.exp(-z * z);
  return 0.5 * (1.0 + sign * y);
}

No dependency on a stats library. Thirty lines of code give you a z-test that matches SciPy to six decimal places.

Wilson confidence intervals

A p-value tells you whether there is a difference. A confidence interval tells you how big the difference might actually be, which is what you want to know when deciding whether to ship.

The naive confidence interval for a proportion uses the normal approximation: . This breaks badly when is near 0 or 1, or when is small, because the interval can go below 0 or above 1. Those bounds are nonsensical: a conversion rate cannot be negative.

The Wilson interval is the fix. It is derived from inverting the z-test and solving for the interval endpoints directly:

function wilsonInterval(
  conversions: number,
  exposures: number,
  z: number = 1.96
): [number, number] {
  if (exposures === 0) return [0, 0];
  const p = conversions / exposures;
  const n = exposures;
  const denominator = 1 + (z * z) / n;
  const centre = p + (z * z) / (2 * n);
  const margin = z * Math.sqrt((p * (1 - p) + (z * z) / (4 * n)) / n);

  return [
    Math.max(0, (centre - margin) / denominator),
    Math.min(1, (centre + margin) / denominator),
  ];
}

is the 95% confidence value. The and terms come from the algebra of inverting the z-test. It still rests on the normal approximation, but because it solves for the endpoints instead of plugging the observed rate into the standard error, the Wilson interval always sits inside [0, 1] and holds up much better than the naive interval at small .

The dashboard shows Wilson intervals as bars on each variant's conversion rate. A variant with 500 exposures and 50 conversions shows a 10% rate with a visibly wide bar. A variant with 50,000 exposures and 5,000 conversions shows a 10% rate with a bar so narrow you can only just see it. The bar is how "how confident am I in this number?" is communicated without a single line of text.

The significance check is applied in :

significant: confidence >= 95,

A winner is then the first significant variant whose lift is positive:

const winner = computed.find((v) => v.significant && (v.lift ?? 0) > 0);

This avoids two common traps. First, declaring a loser as a winner (significant but lift is negative). Second, letting noise promote a marginal variant before the sample is large enough for the test to have real power. The 95% threshold is chosen deliberately; at the standard 5% alpha and typical sample sizes, roughly one in twenty A/A tests will show false significance. If you lower the threshold you will ship winners faster and also ship losers more often.

Wilson intervals and z-tests assume independent trials and fixed sample sizes. They are not sequential-testing-aware. If you peek at an experiment every day and stop as soon as it hits significance, your effective false-positive rate is much higher than 5%. Flip's solution is simple: do not do that. Set a minimum sample size per variant before the test is evaluated, and commit to running for a fixed window. Sequential-testing frameworks (like mSPRT or Bayesian approaches) solve this more elegantly, but add complexity that a personal-project A/B tool does not need.

The SDK is basically nothing

// sdk/flip.ts, roughly
export function decide(visitorId: string, experimentKey: string) {
  const experiment = cache[experimentKey];
  if (!experiment) return { variant: null };
  const variant = assignVariant(visitorId, experimentKey, experiment.variants);
  return { variant };
}

The SDK's job is three things: fetch flag and experiment configuration from the dashboard API, cache it, and call locally. All the logic is in the hashing function, which is shared between dashboard and SDK so assignments match exactly.

The whole SDK compresses to under 2 KB because the hashing function is the only non-trivial part and that function is already small. No websockets, no streaming, no background sync: experiments update when the SDK refetches (every 60 seconds by default), which is plenty fast for decisions that happen at page-view frequency.

A ClickHouse or warehouse integration. Flip uses Postgres for exposure and conversion events. Events are tiny (experiment id, variant, visitor id, timestamp), and the hot queries are aggregations grouped by variant. Postgres is perfectly adequate for a single-product traffic volume.

A dedicated UI framework. The dashboard is Next.js App Router with server components where possible and minimal client state. The charts are just numbers rendered as divs with widths computed from the Wilson intervals. Nothing fancy.

An auth provider. API keys are UUIDs stored hashed. Requests that carry a valid key are trusted for write access; public decide calls do not need auth.

Flip is three hundred lines of meaningful code and a Postgres schema. LaunchDarkly charges a few hundred pounds a month for a feature flag service. I get the one I need for the cost of the Vercel deployment, which is zero because it fits on the free tier. If your product does not have a data scientist reviewing experiments daily, a service like Flip is probably what you actually want.

items.title: I Built an AI Agent Skill That Writes Better YARA-L Detection Rules
items.author: AjayNyayapathi
items.content:
Ask a general purpose AI assistant for a YARA-L brute force rule. You will get something that looks correct. Paste it into the Google SecOps Rules Editor. It fails on line five, because LOGIN is not a valid UDM event type. The correct value is USER_LOGIN.

Fix that. The next error is a port compared to the string "443". Fix that. The compiler complains that an outcome variable uses an event field without an aggregate.

The worst case is the rule that compiles cleanly and never fires. Your Okta parser writes FAIL for a failed login. The rule checks for BLOCK. Nothing errors. Nothing alerts. You find out during an incident review.

I write detection content for a living. I got tired of fixing the same five mistakes in every AI generated rule. So I built yara-l-skill, an open source Agent Skill that teaches coding agents to write, review, tune and convert YARA-L 2.0 rules

An Agent Skill is a folder with a file of instructions, plus any reference docs and scripts the agent needs. The agent loads it when the task matches the skills description. You install it once. Every YARA-L request picks it up automatically.

The same folder works in Claude Code, Claude.ai, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor and any other client that reads the SKILL.md format.

Give your agent a threat description, an ATT&CK technique ID, a Sigma rule or an SPL or KQL query. The skill makes it return six things, in this order:

  1. A single sentence statement of the detection logic
  2. An entire YARA-L 2.0 rule with all meta, outcome and $risk_score
  3. A list of UDM fields to see if you need to validate that the fields are the same on your parser
  4. The reference lists and data tables to prepare, including sample rows
  5. A shall fire test B shall not fire test
  6. The top two false positive offenders and how to tune them out

Items 3-6 are as important as the rule. A rule with no test and no tuning notes is a rule your SOC is going to turn off in week two.

Write a YARA-L rule for 10 failed logins followed by a success within 30 minutes.

The agent first restates the logic: "Alert when one user has 10 or more failed logins followed by a successful login within 30 minutes." Then it picks the rule shape (multi event with match), maps the fields, and writes this:

rule user_login_bruteforce_then_success {

  meta:
    author = "community"
    description = "Ten or more failed logins for one account followed by a successful login inside 30 minutes."
    severity = "HIGH"
    priority = "HIGH"
    mitre_attack_tactic = "Credential Access"
    mitre_attack_technique = "T1110"
    reference = "https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110/"
    false_positives = "Mobile mail clients retrying an expired password, then the user updating it."
    rule_version = "1.0"
    yara_version = "YL2.0"

  events:
    $fail.metadata.event_type = "USER_LOGIN"
    // VERIFY: some parsers write FAIL instead of BLOCK for failed logins.
    $fail.security_result.action = "BLOCK"
    $fail.target.user.userid = $user

    $success.metadata.event_type = "USER_LOGIN"
    $success.security_result.action = "ALLOW"
    $success.target.user.userid = $user

    // The success must come after the failures.
    $fail.metadata.event_timestamp.seconds < $success.metadata.event_timestamp.seconds

    // Tuning hook: service accounts with known retry storms.
    not $user in %bruteforce_excluded_accounts

  match:
    $user over 30m

  outcome:
    $risk_score = 80
    $failed_count = count_distinct($fail.metadata.id)
    $fail_source_ips = array_distinct($fail.principal.ip)
    $success_source_ips = array_distinct($success.principal.ip)

  condition:
    #fail >= 10 and $success
}

A few details in that rule come straight from the skill's instructions:

  • metadata.event_type comes first. It is indexed, so filtering on it early cuts the volume the engine scans.
  • Both event variables join on $user. An unjoined variable in a multi event rule causes a compile error or a cartesian blowup.
  • The exclusion lives in a reference list. Your SOC edits %bruteforce_excluded_accounts instead of the rule itself.
  • Every outcome field uses an aggregate, because the rule has a match section.
  • The uncertain field carries a . The agent tells you what it could not confirm instead of guessing.

Converting from Sigma, SPL, and KQL

Most teams already have detection logic in another language. The skill includes explicit mapping rules:

plus or

match: $x over <timeframe> plus

match: $user over <window> plus in

A data table or reference list

KQL summarize ... by bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)

Two event variables joined on a placeholder

The skill also tells the agent to state which source constructs have no clean YARA-L equivalent. Silently dropping a filter during conversion is how you end up with a noisy rule nobody trusts.

The skill ships lint_rule.py, a Python 3 script with no dependencies. The agent runs it on every rule before it answers, and you can run it yourself in CI.

Here is a rule with the mistakes I see most often in AI generated YARA-L:

rule bad_login_rule {
  meta:
    author = "me"
  events:
    $failmetadataevent_type = "LOGIN"
    $failtargetport = "443"
    $failtargetuseruserid = $user
    $successmetadataevent_type = "USER_LOGIN"
    reregex($failprincipalhostname `.*corp`)
  match:
    $user over 30m
  outcome:
    $src = $failprincipalip
  condition:
    #fail >= 10 and $success
}

$ python3 scripts/lint_rule.py bad.yaral
[FAIL] bad.yaral
  error:   unknown metadata.event_type value "LOGIN"
  error:   integer field ending '.port' compared to a quoted string
  error:   outcome $src uses an event field without an aggregate
  warning: meta missing 'description'
  warning: meta missing 'severity'

  warning: regex starts with .* (slow): .*corp
  warning: $success is not assigned to any match placeholder
  warning: no $risk_score in outcome

It checks section order, event type values against the UDM enum, integer fields compared to strings, event variables that never join to a match placeholder, unaggregated outcome fields, absence conditions without match, leading .* in regex, and missing meta keys.

A clean lint result does not mean the rule compiles. The linter catches the common mistakes before you paste. The SecOps compiler is still the final word.

Parser fixtures: the gap the linter cannot close

Valid syntax and a rule that fires are two separate problems. The linter solves the first one. Fixtures address the second.

A fixture is a JSON file with three things: a sanitized raw log, the UDM event a specific parser produced from it, and the rule that should or should not fire on it. They live in folders by log type:

fixtures/
  AZURE_AD/
    device_code_signin_fire.json
    device_code_signin_approved_no_fire.json
  OKTA/
    bruteforce_then_success_fire.json
    three_fails_then_success_no_fire.json
  WINDOWS_SYSMON/
    certutil_urlcache_download_fire.json
    certutil_hashfile_no_fire.json

confirms every field the rule uses exists in the UDM event, compares literal values and regex conditions, and checks #var thresholds. When a parser writes a different value than the rule expects, you get this:

[FAIL] fixtures/OKTA/bruteforce_then_success_fire.json
  error:   $fail: 0 event(s) match its conditions, rule needs #fail >= 10
  error:     security_result.action: rule wants = 'BLOCK', fixture has ['ALLOW', 'FAIL']

That is the FAIL versus BLOCK problem from the top of this post, caught before deployment.

The checker also rejects fixtures that contain public IPs, real email domains, or real GUIDs, so nobody leaks tenant data in a pull request. When the agent writes a rule for a log source that has fixtures, it reads them first to learn which fields that parser actually fills.

Guardrails built into the skill

I wrote four hard limits into SKILL.md, based on what goes wrong when an AI writes detection content:

  • It never claims a rule compiles. It tells you to validate in the Rules Editor or through the SecOps API.
  • It never invents UDM fields. If a field is not in the reference docs or your sample log, it says so.
  • It never sets a rule to alerting by default. It recommends running live with alerting off for 7 days while you review detection volume.
  • It keeps real hostnames, IPs, and usernames out of shareable examples.

Copy the skills/yara-l-authoring folder into your agent's skill directory:

git clone https://github.com/ajaynyayapathi/yara-l-skill.git
cp -r yara-l-skill/skills/yara-l-authoring ~/.claude/skills/
  • UDM field population varies by parser. That is why // VERIFY: comments and fixtures exist.
  • Every fixture in the first release is synthetic, built from public schema docs, and marked verified_against_tenant: false.
  • The fixture checker is a field and value check. It ignores match windows, timestamp ordering, and reference list contents. Only the SecOps compiler and a retrohunt prove a rule works.
  • Example rules use placeholder list and table names. Replace them before you deploy.

The most useful contribution is a real parser fixture from your tenant. Run a UDM search, copy the raw log and the UDM view, sanitize them with the template, and open a pull request. Setting verified_against_tenant: true on one Okta or Entra ID fixture makes the skill more accurate for every team that uses that parser.

If you do not have time for a PR, open a "Parser mismatch" issue and tell me which value your parser writes.

GitHub Actions runs the linter and fixture checker on every pull request, so contributed rules and fixtures get the same checks the agent runs.
