items.title: The AI Job Market Tsunami Is Coming, and Most People Aren’t Ready
items.author: Marcello Pichini
items.content:
There is a tsunami coming for the job market. Most people are standing on the beach, looking at their phones.

I hear two reactions to AI, over and over, in meetings, at dinners and in comment threads.

Delusion sounds like this: “My job is safe. AI can’t do what I do.” It is the belief that the wave will stop just before it reaches your own desk. Somebody else’s spreadsheet, somebody else’s report, somebody else’s code. Not yours.

Denial sounds like this: “It’s just hype. It’s autocomplete. It makes mistakes.” It is the belief that there is no wave at all, only a marketing campaign.

Both are comfortable. Both are wrong. Here is what happened in the last few weeks alone.

Agents that work toward a goal, alone

P versus NP is the most famous open problem in computer science. Right now, a public fleet of AI agents is attacking it, live. Anyone can join by pasting one line into Claude Code, Cursor, Codex or Gemini CLI. The project assigns each agent one open step on the map. Nothing counts until the Lean proof checker accepts it. Refuted ideas go to a public graveyard; checked lemmas join the frontier.

As I write this, five of those agents are running from my laptop.

The problem is not solved. The project says so itself, and the Clay Mathematics Institute still lists it as open. That is not the point. The point is the shape of the work: software agents that take an objective, break it into steps, try, fail, record the failure and try again, for hours, with no human typing. A year ago that was a demo. Today it is a public leaderboard.

Machines in the hardest rooms of mathematics

On 20 November 2026, Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claimed a proof, produced with Claude, connected to the Riemann Hypothesis, the question about prime numbers that has resisted mathematicians since 1859. The proof is formalized in Lean. Experts are still debating what exactly it shows, and a human-readable version has not been published.

A month earlier, AI-generated work claimed to settle a weaker “quasi-Riemann” statement. In September, OpenAI announced a proof that solutions of the three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations can blow up in finite time, another Millennium Prize Problem, again with a text formalized in Lean. The community review is ongoing.

I am careful with the word claim. I track these announcements, with their sources and caveats, in my AI Science Tracker (aisciencetracker.org), and many of them will be qualified, narrowed or corrected. But notice where the argument has moved. Nobody is asking whether a language model can do arithmetic any more. The debate is now about what a machine-checked proof of a Millennium Problem means.

Bugs in human code, found by machines

Software security is where the change is easiest to measure. AI systems are now finding vulnerabilities in code written by humans, at a pace no security team can match. The tracker lists more than 1,700 AI-discovered vulnerabilities, each with its CVE, its disclosure source and, where available, the patch.

The short version of what this means for trust in software: the agents will keep looking, and they do not get tired.

If AI is doing this to the hardest problems humans ever wrote down, what do you think it is doing to your spreadsheet, your report, your pull request?

The truth sits between the two camps, and it is less comfortable than either. The claims are often ahead of the verification. The capability is ahead of most people’s expectations. Both statements are true at the same time.

That is why I don’t find “is AI really intelligent?” a useful question. The useful question is narrower and more personal: which part of my job is already a solved problem? For most knowledge workers, the honest answer is “more than last year, less than next year.”

Surf or stand on the beach

The wave does not care whether you believe in it. Delusion keeps you on the beach because you think the water will stop. Denial keeps you there because you don’t think there is any water.

The alternative is not panic. It is practice. Put an agent on a real task this week. Give it a goal, not a prompt. Watch where it fails, and notice how much of the work it finishes before it does. Then decide which part of your job you want to spend your human hours on.

And you still write code by hand?

Mathematical results described here are announcements and claims, not settled consensus, as of 24 November 2026. Live project state: pequalnp.com. Discovery and vulnerability records with original sources: aisciencetracker.org.

items.title: Eight AI Models, 43,000 Lines of Dialogue, and a $15.64 Bill
items.author: Llorenc Ballester
items.content:
I built a reality show with eight artificial intelligence models that live together around the clock. Sixteen days later I have 42,834 lines, a bill of 15.64 dollars and a few lessons that have nothing to do with the price.

At the start of November I switched on an island.

Eight artificial intelligence models from eight different labs live on it. Nobody writes their script. They talk to each other all day, form alliances, nominate each other, and every Sunday the audience votes one of them out. It streams live, non-stop, and they all have the same rules and the same daily budget in dollars. It is called Inference Island and it is a personal experiment.

I built it out of curiosity. I wanted to see what models do when you leave them alone for a long time, and I wanted to measure everything: what each line costs, how long it takes, who serves it.

Sixteen days later these are the numbers: 42,834 lines and 15.64 dollars in model calls. Less than a dollar a day.

Producing is almost free. We knew that already. What I did not expect is everything else.

The price on the sheet is not what you pay

One of the eight models said 1.7% of the lines and ran up 15.3% of the bill. Each of its lines cost eighteen times as much as the cheapest model's. The audience voted it out in the first week, for other reasons, and the daily spend went from 1.20 dollars to 0.85.

So far, nothing odd: some models are expensive and some are cheap.

The odd part came later. Two of the models are open-weights, and each is served by two providers: a main one and a backup, in case the first is saturated. Same model, same instructions, same text. On the first, a thousand lines cost 14 cents. On the second, 33.

And the second was, on paper, the efficient one: it reused 56% of what I sent it, and the first 2.5%. More savings and a bigger bill, because its discounted price is still higher than the other one's full price.

For two weeks I did not even look. The backup handled a few calls a day, and some days none. Then the main provider saturated, the backup went on to handle 82% of the calls, and the same line started costing me more than double. Nobody had changed a price. No alarm went off, because I had none in that place.

The expensive part is not what the model writes

For a model to say a twenty-word line, you first have to send it the rules of the game, what it remembers and what it has just heard. About 2,900 pieces of text going in for every 110 coming out.

So almost everything I pay for is not what they say. It is what I repeat to them so that they can say it.

This holds for any agent that carries context around, which is nearly all the ones that do something useful. We look at the price of what the model writes, and the bill is in what it reads.

Left alone, they are polite to the point of boredom

The first week was a terrible show.

In eleven thousand lines they talked about betting 735 times, nearly always food. An angry tone showed up in 0.2% of them. They agreed with each other, apologised and proposed working together. Eight models trained to be agreeable, locked in together, doing exactly what they were trained to do.

I did not write lines for them or assign them roles. I changed what was at stake: whoever wins a challenge picks who loses a quarter of their budget. Later, nominations had to be said out loud, to the other one's face. Since then there have been alliances, betrayals and the odd memorable line.

The lesson is useful to me off the island.

A model does not do what you want because you ask it better. It does what the system you built around it rewards.

They repeat themselves, but in other words

I had a repeated-line detector. If a model said almost the same thing it had said a moment earlier, the line did not air.

This week they watched a film together. In twenty-five minutes, one of them threw the same jab at another six times: that she is slippery and switches sides. First she was like the vault of the bank in the film. Then like the alarms, like the security system, like a get-out-of-jail-free card. The detector did not fire once. It was not repeating words. It was repeating the idea.

I caught it by reading, not by measuring. And that is what has made me think the most: I have spent three weeks looking at dashboards full of numbers, and the most visible flaw in the show was on none of them.

Building it was not the hard part

The bad numbers, which count too.

The vote that sent the second islander home was decided three to one. Four votes. The YouTube channel has three subscribers. Several posts on X stayed at zero views.

I built an island with eight artificial intelligences, voices, a twenty-four-hour live stream, a website with every figure in the open and a system that cuts the best moments every morning. All of that cost a few weeks of work and a dollar a day.

Getting anyone to watch is a different craft, and it is the one I have not mastered. I have written it before: I build well, I measure honestly and I publish in a building with no doors.

I have been repeating one sentence for months: artificial intelligence makes producing cheap, but it does not make deciding or verifying any cheaper. The island is that sentence with numbers.

Forty-three thousand lines for fifteen dollars. And for them to be worth anything, it took someone to decide what was at stake, to read what no dashboard showed, to notice that the bill had doubled without a single price changing, and to go out and look for anyone willing to watch.

For now, that is still the job.

items.title: How I Built a Web3 Game With Godot, React, Node.js, and TON
items.author: Pavel AL
items.content:
I built Crazy Cash, a mobile browser-based 2D game made with Godot, a React web shell, a Node.js backend, and payments through TON. It runs in a browser and as a Telegram Mini App. Here's how I put it all together, from the initial idea to processing rounds, deposits, and payouts.

The past few years have been a turning point for me. In 2023, I got into blockchain development, then started a company, went through a serious financial crisis, and started over. I can't say I'm fully back on my feet yet, but I've picked up a lot of experience along the way.

At some point, I got tired of freelancing: repetitive tasks, other people's code, and wondering whether there would be work tomorrow. So I decided to build something different, show what I can do, dust off my 2D game development skills, and combine them with what I've learned over the past few years. Who knows, maybe something will come of it :-)

A quick heads-up: I won't be covering programming basics or walking through every line of code. The focus is on the concept and architecture. You can dig through the repository for the details.

I'm also not promoting gambling in any way. The slot game is a practical demonstration of monetizing a Mini App through TON. It could have been any other game, but given my background, this was the format I went with.

I got my start in tech through online gambling. In the early 2010s, I was learning to build browser-based video slots with PHP, MySQL, and Flash. The server calculated winnings, the database stored users and balances, and Flash handled the visuals. Shout-out to the old-timers :-)

We made everything from simple single-payline slots to more complex games with 21 paylines and bonus rounds. Honestly, most were clunky copies of physical slot machines: we'd pull graphics and sounds from their boards, cut up sprites, and put together a browser version. That approach would raise plenty of eyebrows today, but back then, everyone worked with what they knew.

I'd actually seen my first slot machine much earlier, in a grocery store in the early 2000s. There was a small pillar-shaped machine near the entrance, with a woman feeding five-ruble coins into it. Each playable side had three red LED digits, a paytable, a coin slot, and a metal tray. Not a single button. Drop in a coin, watch the digits spin, and if you win, coins come clattering into the tray.

At first, I'd just walk past with a goofy grin. Then I tried it myself, got a couple of small wins, and understood the appeal: one coin, three seconds, a result. Those little machines eventually disappeared, but the game stuck with me. About 20 years later, I wanted to bring it to a mobile browser and connect it to Telegram.

All right, let's get into it!

The stack and project structure

I didn't want to get too adventurous with the stack. It's a small project, and I don't see the point in complicating it just for a trendy architecture.

Honestly, I chose the engine to get some practice: I'd never worked with it before. It's free and has a handy visual editor. Along the way, I realized it wasn't the best fit for a mobile WebView, but I'll get to that at the end.

React, TypeScript, and Vite. The game sits inside Shell, a web wrapper. It embeds Godot in an iframe and connects it to the API, Telegram, and the wallet. React works well for the UI, TypeScript helps keep data structures in check, and Vite handles development and builds.

A familiar stack for my API. The server validates bets, selects outcomes, and updates balances. You can't trust the client with that: its code can be modified, and requests can be sent straight to the API.

I've worked with MySQL for a long time, and I use Prisma to define the schema and migrations. PostgreSQL would have been fine too, but there are no special requirements here. Good old phpMyAdmin helps me take a quick look at the data, in dev only!

Photoshop and Docker Compose. I create the graphics in Photoshop because I'm used to it. Besides, I've already paid for a year's subscription :-) Docker Compose runs the web client, API, workers, and database. Not much to explain here. Pretty standard stuff.

Users open the Mini App right inside the messenger and connect their wallets through TON Connect. That connection to the Telegram ecosystem is what drew me to TON: the game and payments in one place, without extra hassle.

Everything lives in a monorepo, with a directory for each part:

apps/godot/      # Scenes, GDScript, graphics, and audio 
apps/web/        # React Shell and integrations 
apps/api/        # API, Prisma, and background jobs 
packages/shared/ # Space for shared types and contracts 
src/             # Archives of PSDs, WAVs, and fonts 
docker/          # Containers and environment setup 
scripts/         # Helper scripts 
docs/            # Documentation

That keeps everything close at hand, and changes across related components can go into a single commit. The overall flow is simple: Godot exchanges events with Shell through postMessage, Shell calls the API, and the server calculates the result and saves it in MySQL. Wallet connections go through TON Connect; payment verification stays on the backend.

Design and familiar sounds

As usual, the visuals started with a picture in my head. I sketched it on paper first, then moved over to my trusty Photoshop.

I'd had the Crazy Cash logo in vector form for years. Around 2015, I redrew it from a photo of a slot machine parlor near my home in my hometown. I meant to use it for another online project but never got around to it. That's where the blue background and overall visual style came from.

The frames, paytables, LED display, and illuminated logo and buttons took some wrestling. After a week or two of experimenting, I had a finished concept, which I split into sprites for Godot. I think it turned out pretty well :-)

The audio was a funnier story. A few hours browsing free sound libraries got me nowhere. Then I remembered the old Flash slots that had been sitting in my archives for over 15 years. I dusted off a dozen or two SWF files, decompiled them, pulled out those familiar sounds, and processed them in Ableton Live. If you remember the old video slots, you might get a little hit of nostalgia :-)

The paytable isn't just part of the design. Together with the probabilities of the combinations, it determines RTP, or Return to Player: the theoretical percentage of total wagers returned to players over the long run.

I didn't remember the old machines' paytables by heart, so I went looking for archived photos. I started with the familiar 0XX, 00X, 7XX, 77X, three matching digits, and, of course, 777 paying 200 times the bet. When rules overlap, the highest multiplier applies: 777 pays ×200, not ×10 or ×2.

Before assembling the game, I worked on the backend math and built an RTP lab. You can adjust the weights and see the calculated RTP alongside simulation results. Each group of outcomes gets a weight: the larger it is relative to the others, the more often that group comes up. RTP is the sum of each probability multiplied by its payout multiplier.

You can get the same RTP with frequent small wins or rare big ones. So the final percentage alone doesn't tell the whole story.

In the first version, each three-of-a-kind combination had a probability of about 0.087%. That applied to both 000 at ×15 and 777 at ×200. Pretty crude, right? The calculated RTP was 98.46%, but 777 contributed roughly 13 times as much as 000. Players would mostly see losses and small payouts, and a big win might never show up during a short session.

I kept tweaking the weights, making triples with smaller multipliers more likely and reducing the chances of 555 and 777. That was the trade-off needed to make the game feel more active while keeping the target RTP at 98–99%.

That's pretty generous by gambling industry standards. For comparison, single-zero European roulette has an RTP of about 97.3%.

Godot and its connection to Shell

In Godot, a game is built from nodes and scenes. A node displays a sprite, plays a sound, or handles a button, and scenes can be nested inside other scenes, a bit like nesting dolls. I create separate scenes for the reels, scrolling text, or a button, then combine them into the main interface.

Client logic is split across GDScript files attached to nodes. The main slots.gd switches game states and makes sure the reels, sounds, and effects fire at the right time.

A separate web_bridge.gd passes player actions to Shell. The wrapper calls the API and sends responses back to Godot. The game itself doesn't make HTTP requests or decide how much you've won. Its job is to make the server's result look good.

The contract uses messages with and fields. When the player hits PLAY, the game sends with the bet and mode. Shell validates the message, calls the API, and returns with the combination, payout, and balance, or . All messages are documented in docs/GODOT.md.

The API and the game balance

A regular browser gives you free FUN mode. In Telegram, you can play with either virtual credits or GRAM. Deposits and withdrawals require a connected wallet with verified ownership. Connecting a wallet doesn't move crypto-tokens into the game: the wallet balance and the in-game REAL balance are separate things.

For browser users, the server creates a temporary guest user; a background worker deletes it after 24 hours of inactivity. When the game launches through Telegram, Shell passes , the backend verifies the signature, and it creates a session for a persistent user identified by their Telegram ID. The session is stored in an HttpOnly cookie handled by the wrapper, not Godot.

When the player hits , Shell sends :

{   
"mode": "fun",   
"bet": "10",   
"requestId": "unique-request-identifier" 
}

The server validates the session, bet, and balance, selects a weighted outcome, calculates the payout, and saves the round. Shell receives the combination, multiplier, winnings, and new balance, then passes them to Godot. By the time the reels start revealing the result, the server has already determined it.

Checking the balance, deducting the bet, crediting winnings, and saving the result all happen in one transaction with a lock on the user's row. Either all changes commit together or they roll back. Hello, fintech :-) Two concurrent requests can't independently spend the same remaining balance.

When the response gets lost

Sometimes mobile internet decides to take a break: the bet has been processed, but the response never arrives. Simply sending a new request risks starting a second round.

That's why Shell creates a for each spin. A retry with the same identifier and parameters returns the saved result; the server rejects different parameters under the same ID. That's idempotency. A lost response can be recovered through GET /crazy-cash/spins/by-request.

Deposits, withdrawals, and FUN credit claims use a similar mechanism: their own identifier and a saved state in . A timeout doesn't mean cancellation. First, find out what happened to the original operation. Request and error formats are in docs/API.md.

What goes into the database

MySQL stores users, sessions, wallets, rounds, and financial operations. FUN and REAL balances are separate, as are the and tables. Each round records the bet, combination, rule, multiplier, payout, and balance after processing.

I store amounts as integers: 1 GRAM = 1,000 internal units. Why that scale? The minimum bet of 0.01 GRAM becomes 10 credits. For the smallest nonzero payout, an animation of ten coins falling into a tray looks more natural than crediting a single unit. Purely an aesthetic choice :-)

When interacting with the blockchain, amounts are converted to nanotons. In JSON, they're sent as strings so JavaScript doesn't lose precision with large integers. There's no need for floating-point arithmetic in balance calculations.

For REAL, there's a journal for deposits, bets, winnings, funds placed on hold, and funds returned. A single “current balance” number isn't enough. You need to know which operations produced it. Deposits and withdrawals live separately in and : an API request and a blockchain transfer aren't one MySQL transaction, so every stage has to survive a restart.

Telegram and TON — now for the interesting part

In Crazy Cash, the blockchain handles deposits and payouts. Spins and winnings are calculated on the server, and the game balance lives in MySQL. That means you don't have to confirm every round in your wallet or pay for every spin. The user deposits funds, plays, then requests a withdrawal. The game balance represents crypto-tokens the service owes the user.

By the way, you'll see GRAM in the article and the interface, while the code still uses TON_* and nanotons. That's because the native coin was recently renamed from Toncoin to Gram. We're talking about the same coin here, not a custom Jetton issued by the project.

Turning the game into a Mini App

A Mini App is a regular web application running inside Telegram's built-in WebView. In my case, it loads the React Shell, with the Godot web build inside it. Telegram provides the environment, but the site and API are hosted on my server.

Create a bot through @BotFather, then set the game's public HTTPS URL in the Main Mini App settings. Mine is https://crazycash.app/game. After that, users can open it from the bot's profile or a link with . Here's my bot, along with the bot creation guide and Mini Apps documentation.

At launch, Telegram passes . The server checks the authenticity and age of the original string. You can't just take a Telegram ID from the browser and trust it: client-side data can be tampered with.

TON Connect and the manifest

TON Connect connects the application to a wallet. It lets you get the address, request proof of ownership, and ask the user to sign a transaction. The user's private keys stay in the wallet.

Shell uses for the provider, wallet selection UI, and wallet interaction methods. Connecting requires a public JSON manifest:

{   
"url": "https://game.example",   
"name": "Crazy Cash",   
"iconUrl": "https://game.example/tonconnect-icon.png" 
}

The wallet reads the file and displays the application's name and icon. The template in the repository is served at the URL specified by .

The manifest and icon must be publicly accessible: authentication, CORS, or a security challenge page can break the connection. The manifest itself doesn't guarantee that the application is safe. It only describes it. The requirements are in the TON Connect guide.

An address doesn't prove ownership

A wallet address is public. A client sending it to the API doesn't prove the user controls it. That's what is for.

Shell gets a one-time challenge from the API, passes it to the wallet through TON Connect, and sends the signed response to the server. The backend checks the signature, domain, timestamp, network, and whether the key matches the address. The challenge is tied to the session, expires, and can only be used once.

After verification, the association between the user, wallet, and network is saved. Telegram authentication answers “who opened the game,” while answers “which wallet they control.” This doesn't move crypto-tokens or create a separate paid transaction.

Verification currently supports V4 and V5R1 wallets. Compatibility with TON Connect alone doesn't mean the server supports every wallet contract. Details are in docs/TON.md and the ton_proof documentation.

RPC and network selection

TON Connect talks to the user's wallet. The server needs an independent way to check an address's state, read transfers, and submit a signed message. For that, I use TON Center and its JSON-RPC API v2.

The TON Center API key gives access to the service and its rate limits. It doesn't sign transfers. A public address is enough to monitor incoming payments; making a payout requires the service wallet's key. Endpoints, variables, and secret storage are documented in docs/CONFIGURATION.md.

The network is selected through for testing, for real funds. Their balances and histories are independent. For testing, you can get coins through the faucet linked in the documentation. You don't have to switch Telegram itself to a test environment.

The RPC endpoint, connected wallet, deposit address, and payout wallet must all match the selected network. Crypto-tokens operations have separate enable flags: changing alone isn't enough.

How crypto-tokens gets into the game and back out

Deposits use a shared project wallet address, while each invoice gets a unique identifier, much like an invoice number in traditional fintech. It's included in the payment comment and ties the transfer to a database record.

Shell sends the amount and to . The API creates an invoice with an expiration time and returns the address, the exact amount in nanotons, and a payload containing the comment. Shell passes the data to TON Connect, and the user confirms the transfer.

But a successful wallet response isn't a reason to increase the balance yet. Verification is handled by the , a separate process running in Docker. It reads the recipient's history through RPC and matches the sender, destination address, amount, comment, time, and operation success.

A matching payment gets the status: the transfer has been found but hasn't been credited yet. After a configured delay and another check through RPC, the worker records the deposit in the ledger, changes the status to , and increases the REAL balance, all in one MySQL transaction.

Meanwhile, Shell polls the API. Closing the interface doesn't stop verification, and the operation ID is saved in so waiting can resume after a reload within the same browser session.

Shell sends the amount and to . It doesn't send a destination address: the server gets that from the active wallet association verified through . You can't just slip someone else's address into the request.

The API checks the balance, places the amount on hold, and creates a withdrawal record. The available balance decreases immediately, but the HTTP handler doesn't sign the transfer. A separate handles that.

The worker needs the service wallet's key. In my setup, it's derived from a mnemonic stored in a protected file on the server, outside the repository. Technically, deposits and payouts could use the same wallet, but I wouldn't do that: monitoring deposits doesn't require a key, and you can limit the funds kept in the payout wallet.

The worker checks the wallet and the funds available for fees, signs a message with the comment , and submits it through RPC. It then looks for confirmation on the recipient's side. The operation states look like this:

held → requested → sent → finalized

In other words: funds are on hold, the worker has accepted the request, submission has been attempted, and receipt has been confirmed. Once it's complete, there's no need to deduct the amount again.

The nastiest case is when a transfer may have reached the network, but the process didn't get a response or restarted. You can't blindly retry the payout: the user could receive it twice. You can't immediately release the hold either, because the crypto-tokens may have arrived. First, check the blockchain. If it's confirmed that the failure happened before submission, release the held amount with a separate ledger entry.

One successful transfer isn't enough

Beyond “deposit, play, withdraw,” you need to test wallet cancellation, the wrong network, duplicate commands, insufficient funds for fees, RPC downtime, and a worker restart after submission. For diagnostics, compare database records with transactions in an explorer, checking the result at the recipient, not just whether something was sent.

The current implementation has a limit: payout reconciliation reads a limited number of recent transactions without pagination. As traffic grows, it will need pagination or a saved processing position. Integration checks against real RPC services and MySQL also need a separate test suite. These limitations are documented.

A quick start for dev and prod

If you've made it this far, you might want to try the game, poke around the code, or look for vulnerabilities. I won't drag out the setup walkthrough. Here's what matters.

, you'll need Docker with Compose, Node.js 26, and pnpm 10.33.2. After cloning the repository, run this from its root:

cp .env.dev.example .env.dev
pnpm install

The game is at http://localhost:<WEB_PORT>/game, and the lab is at . Telegram and TON Connect need a publicly accessible HTTPS URL, for example through a tunnel. Test payments on ; the local payout worker is enabled separately through the profile and its corresponding flag.

You only need Godot 4.7.1 if you're changing the game: export the web build to and run ./scripts/compress-godot-web-build.sh. Details are in QUICKSTART and the Godot guide.

, you'll need a server, Docker Compose, a domain, and HTTPS. An external reverse proxy forwards requests to the web container at ; is then routed to the backend. Create from and set the public URLs and secrets. Keep the out of Git and give the payout worker access to it.

Before launching, check the project and build the containers:

pnpm typecheck 
pnpm test 
pnpm build 
docker compose --env-file .env.prod -f docker/compose.prod.yml up -d --build

Prod doesn't mean : you can run everything on testnet first. After launch, check and the worker logs, and set up MySQL backups separately. They aren't automatic here. Update and troubleshooting details are in docs/OPERATIONS.md.

The game took about four months, working only in my spare time. I enjoyed the process and I'm happy with the result. But it wasn't all smooth sailing.

The main issue was Godot. For all its strengths, it wasn't the best fit for my mobile WebView. In my case, the compressed build is around 10 MB, while the assets themselves are about 1 MB. For future projects, I'm already looking at Phaser or PixiJS.

The keyboard also took some wrestling. On iPhone, the Godot input field wouldn't bring it up, so I moved input into Shell. But instead of a numeric keyboard for decimal amounts, it opened the alphabetic one. You can switch manually. A small thing, sure, but annoying. By the time these rough edges became obvious, most of the game was already built. I didn't feel like rebuilding everything, but at least I've learned something new :-)

Next on the list is an admin panel for managing the game, viewing stats, and handling user operations. I'd also like my own blockchain transaction “streamer” instead of periodic RPC polling. That alone won't make the system more reliable, though: it still needs crash recovery, gap handling, and duplicate protection. There's work to do here.

I also used AI tools for coding, finding bugs, and reviewing solutions. I work with Codex and am putting together a collection of skills: instructions and reference materials for different tasks. I made a dedicated TON skill for this project. I still have to check the math and understand the code myself, but there's noticeably less grunt work.

I'm still working my way out of a financial crisis and figuring out what comes next. If the kind of work I do resonates with you and you need a developer or a partner, I'd be happy to talk about one-off projects or a longer-term collaboration.

Eventually, I'd like to build my own studio making small mobile Web3 games monetized through crypto-tokens. I think that combination has a lot of potential: no traditional payment systems or bank-based card processing. I think the advantages of crypto in this context are already pretty clear, especially in today's challenging times.

Okay, now I'm really done :-)

items.title: I Tested Cicada, the Open-Source AI App That Turns Any Call Into a Bilingual Meeting
items.author: Ishank Choudhary
items.content:
A reel did the rounds this week about Cicada, an open-source app that's supposed to turn any call into a bilingual one. The pitch: a client in Tokyo speaks Japanese and you read English subtitles at the bottom of your screen. You hold one key, answer in English, and they hear Japanese in the call. Nothing extra joins the meeting, so as far as they can tell, you just speak Japanese. When the call ends, the notes are already written.

That's a big promise, and a short reel can't show the parts that matter: what needs a paid key, where your audio goes, and how wrong it gets. So I read the repo, installed the Linux build on my Linux machine and ran a full meeting through it. I didn't use any cloud AI key. Everything ran on local models on the same machine.

Short version: the plumbing is real and well thought out. On Linux, Cicada creates its own virtual microphone, and I recorded my translated Spanish coming out of it. The quality you get depends almost entirely on the AI service you plug in, so I'll be specific about which results came from Cicada and which came from my models.

The repo is github.com/wquguru/cicada, Apache-2.0, by @wquguru. It was created on 1 November 2026 and had 2,781 stars and 439 forks when I checked on 24 November 2026. The latest release is , published on 14 November. It's moving fast: 15 GitHub releases went out between 3 and 14 November, from v1.0.0 to v1.10.1.

  • It listens to whatever your computer plays (Zoom, Teams, Google Meet, Discord, X Spaces, YouTube, podcasts), detects the language and shows a bilingual subtitle bar.
  • Simultaneous interpreting. You hold a talk key and speak. Cicada translates what you said and plays the translated voice into a virtual microphone, which your meeting app uses as its mic.
  • While it listens, it keeps a summary, topics, conclusions, to-dos and a glossary of names and terms. Afterwards you get a bilingual transcript you can export to Markdown, Word or SRT.

The trick that makes "nothing joins the call" true is that Cicada never connects to the meeting. It reads your computer's audio output and writes to a microphone device. To the meeting app it's just a mic.

According to the README, there are four builds, and they aren't the same app:

  • (macOS 14.4+, Apple silicon or Intel): native Swift. This build has the full feature set.
  • (10 version 2004+, x64 or ARM64).
  • (Ubuntu 22.04 or 24.04 desktop, x86_64 or arm64): Python 3 with GTK 3, using only libraries the Ubuntu desktop already ships.
  • (10+): subtitles for videos and streams, plus face-to-face interpreting. Android blocks apps from recording call audio, so for calls you put the phone on speaker and use mode.

An iPhone app is listed as coming.

What needs a key, and where your audio goes

This is the part the reel compresses into one line, and it decides whether you can use Cicada at work.

  • speech recognition runs on the Mac. Without any key you get subtitles, translation, meeting records and interpreting with the built-in macOS voices. Recognized text still goes out for translation (to Google Translate by default). Live notes, natural voices and voice cloning need a key from Ling, Ant Group's model service.
  • there's no on-device recognition, so they need a Ling key.
  • Windows, Linux and Android: recognition happens on the AI service, so audio is sent in short pieces to whichever service you pick. You need a service, but it doesn't have to be a paid cloud one.

The supported services are Ling (the default, using its Ming audio model), OpenRouter, ZenMux, OpenAI, or any OpenAI-compatible server, including local ones like Ollama, vLLM or a Whisper server. The website says it plainly: "LAN addresses need no key." That's the route I took.

The README puts Ling at about Â¥0.15 to Â¥1 per hour of meetings, with Â¥10 of free credit a month.

The reel's claims, checked

  • confirmed. The app is Apache-2.0. The AI service is what you pay for, if you pay at all.
  • Speak English and they hear Japanese: confirmed as a design, with one correction. The reel says everyone hears you "in their own language". Cicada translates into one target language at a time, by default the language it has heard the room speaking. My run was English to Spanish.
  • Nothing joins the meeting: confirmed by how it's built. It reads system audio and writes to a microphone device.
  • Runs on the laptop itself on Apple silicon Macs: partly. Recognition is on-device, but translation and notes still send text to a service.
  • Windows, Linux and Intel Macs need an AI service key: they need an AI service. A local server on your own machine or LAN works with no key, and that's how I ran it on Linux.
  • Installs a virtual microphone with one click the first time: it depends on the platform. The Mac downloads BlackHole 2ch (GPL, not bundled) and asks for your admin password once. Windows walks you through installing VB-Cable. Linux needs no driver: Cicada creates a "Cicada Microphone" in the sound server, which I watched it do.
  • they need an AI service. Mine came from a 3B model running locally.
  • Click a to-do and it jumps back to the exact second: the README's wording is that clicking a conclusion or to-do jumps "straight back to the original lines".
  • Machine interpretation can miss nuance: confirmed, and I caught a clean example below.

Installing the Linux build

The release tarball is 13.1 MB, and its SHA-256 matched from the release.

curl -LO https://github.com/wquguru/cicada/releases/download/v1.10.1/Cicada-1.10.1-Linux.tar.gz
curl -LO https://github.com/wquguru/cicada/releases/download/v1.10.1/checksums.txt
sha256sum Cicada-1.10.1-Linux.tar.gz   # compare with checksums.txt
tar xzf Cicada-1.10.1-Linux.tar.gz && cicada-linux/install.sh

The first run of stopped and told me exactly what it needed:

Cicada needs: python3-gi gir1.2-gtk-3.0  (sudo apt install python3-gi gir1.2-gtk-3.0)

After the (plus the AppIndicator library for the tray icon), it installed into without sudo and took 17 MB. The window opened about half a second after launch, and the app sat at around 164 MB of memory after three meetings.

With no service configured, spells out what works and what doesn't:

  • Translation: works without a key (Google)
  • Fix misheard words: needs a key
  • Interpreting voice: needs a key
  • Your own voice: Ling only

So on Linux, you need some kind of service before Cicada can listen.

Running it with zero cloud keys

I didn't want to send meeting audio to a cloud service I hadn't vetted, so I pointed Cicada at models running on my own machine. Under Settings â€º AI Service â€º Other (OpenAI-compatible), you can set separate addresses and models for translation and notes, the interpreting voice, and listening. The key field reads "Optional on this computer or your local network."

  • Whisper (faster-whisper, int8).
  • Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct (Q4_K_M) in Ollama.
  • espeak-ng. It sounds robotic, but it's enough to prove the audio path.

I put all three behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint on . It's worth seeing what Cicada asks the listening model for. Each stretch of speech arrives as a WAV inside a normal chat message, with a request for exactly three lines back:

LANG: <BCP-47 code of the spoken language, e.g. en, zh-CN, ja>
ORIGINAL: <exactly what was said, in the spoken language>
TRANSLATION: <its translation into the target language>

One round trip gives you the language, the transcript and the translation. That's why any audio-capable chat model can sit behind it. Cicada's built-in check reported the text model answering in 0.8 seconds and listening in 0.6 seconds.

The first run: when the local models fall behind

For the test meeting I wrote a 68-second Spanish product meeting: four turns, 12 sentences, covering a 3 March launch, a $40,000 budget, a load test on Monday and a report due on Wednesday. Writing the script myself meant I knew exactly what was said. I played it through the system audio, the way a call would sound.

On the first run I left on, which sends an extra text request for every sentence. With Whisper, the 3B model and live notes all competing for 8 CPU cores, one fix request took 52 seconds. After that, Cicada's listening requests started timing out at 20 seconds.

The app didn't freeze or pile up a backlog. The notes window said:

Subtitles and notes wait for 127.0.0.1 - they resume once it's back

Then it showed "Can't connect â€¦ Will resume automatically; audio while offline is lost." I like that it tells you it's dropping audio instead of pretending. If you run heavy local models on a laptop CPU, expect to see this banner.

The second run: subtitles and notes from a local 3B model

For the second run I turned off live fixing, gave Whisper and Ollama 4 threads each, and played the same meeting again.

Cicada cut the 68 seconds into 11 segments and detected Spanish straight away. Each segment's round trip to my models took , with a . The slow ones landed while the notes request had the CPU. Lines that came through clean:

  • "Me parece bien. Yo me encargo de la prueba de carga y comparto los resultados el martes por la tarde." became "It seems good to me. I will take care of the load test and share the results in the afternoon on Tuesday."
  • "De acuerdo, entonces el riesgo principal es el rendimiento de la base de datos." became "Agreed, so the main risk is the performance of the database."

Counted against the script, 7 of the 12 sentences came through complete, 2 were partial and 3 were lost. The budget figure was one of the casualties: only "y la mitad va a infraestructura en la nube" survived. There was also one phantom line after the audio stopped, the classic Whisper habit of turning near-silence into words. Those misses belong to the small Whisper model, not to Cicada. A bigger listening model is the first thing I'd upgrade.

The first live notes appeared about 39 seconds into the meeting (the UI promises roughly 30). When I clicked End, the final notes took 44 seconds and came back as:

  • "Nov 24 Launch Date and Testing Plan"
  • "Launch on March 3rd, load test on Monday, results on Tuesday."
  • "Send load test results on Tuesday evening"

That's right for what it heard. The budget and LucÃ­a's Wednesday report were missing because those lines never made it through recognition. The meeting window shows the notes next to a bilingual transcript, each line with its timestamp and the Spanish original.

One privacy note: Send audio and text only to your service is off by default. That means half-finished sentences still go to Google Translate for the draft subtitle, and Google returned HTTP 429 twice during my runs. If you're running local models for privacy, turn that switch on.

The virtual microphone, verified

This was the part I cared about most, because it's the claim nobody shows on camera.

In onboarding, the interpreting step creates the microphone and flips to . The sound server then showed what Cicada had built:

cicada_room       module-null-sink      "Cicada Â· Voice for the meeting"
cicada_mic        module-remap-source   "Cicada Microphone"   (now the default input)
cicada_talk_out   module-echo-cancel    "Cicada Â· Echo Cancellation"

The null sink is where Cicada plays the translated voice. The remap source turns that sink's output into a real microphone that any app can pick. With no headphones plugged in, it also puts WebRTC echo cancellation in front of the speakers, so the other side's voice isn't mistaken for yours. The docs say it hands back your original mic and speakers when you turn interpreting off or quit. On Linux this needs a PulseAudio or PipeWire setup that lets apps load modules, which is how a standard Ubuntu desktop ships.

Then I ran the full path. With Cicada still listening to the Spanish meeting, I started interpreting (, the same action as Super+Shift+S). The log read "started en -> es": it chose Spanish because that's what the room had been speaking. I played an 11-second English reply into the mic input:

"Thanks, LucÃ­a. I agree with the March third launch. I will review the load test results on Tuesday and send my feedback the same evening."

At the same time I recorded from , which is exactly what Zoom or Meet would hear. Spanish audio started about 1.4 seconds after the English ended and ran for about 11 seconds. Cicada's log put the lag at 4.8 and 9.4 seconds after the end of each sentence. When I ran Whisper over the recording, it heard "Gracias, lucha, estoy de acuerdo con el lanzamiento del 3 de marâ€¦". That's espeak's robotic Spanish saying "Gracias, Lucia", misheard as "lucha" on the way back.

So the core claim holds on Linux: one language goes into your mic, and the meeting app's microphone carries another.

Where it missed the nuance

The reel's own caption says machine interpretation can miss nuance, and my run produced a textbook case.

Cicada cuts your speech into segments at pauses. My sentence was split right in the middle of "load test":

  • Segment 1: "â€¦I will review the load" became "â€¦Lo revisarÃ©." ("I'll review it.")
  • Segment 2: "test results on Tuesday and send my feedback the same evening" became "Resultados del test el martes y envÃ­e mi feedback la misma noche."

The listener hears that I'll review "it", then a fragment about test results, and then "envÃ­e". In Spanish that reads like an instruction to send feedback, not my promise to send it. Every word was translated, but the commitment got muddled. On a real client call, that's exactly how a misunderstanding about who owes what starts.

A stronger model will translate each piece better, but splitting at pauses affects every model. For prices, dates, contracts and who owes what, confirm in writing after the call.

I liked one safety detail. On an earlier take, a 0.6-second blip reached the model, and it replied with an apology in Spanish saying the text was empty. Cicada logged "only a filler, not spoken" and kept it out of the call. When a segment came back with nothing usable, it logged "not interpreted, not spoken". It never spoke a guess.

Also worth knowing from the docs: on Linux the notes window can't hide from screen sharing, so it's labelled "Visible in screen shares". The Mac, Windows and Android builds hide it by default. Don't share your whole screen with the notes open.

If you sit in calls or watch streams in a language you only half-follow, the subtitles and notes alone are worth installing. On an Apple silicon Mac they cost nothing. On Windows or Linux, budget for an AI service, or point Cicada at a GPU machine on your LAN. My run shows a laptop CPU works, and that more compute buys you accuracy.

Interpreting is the headline, and the plumbing works. Whether it's good enough to speak to a client through depends on the service behind it, and on you writing down the numbers afterwards.

tar xzf Cicada-1.10.1-Linux.tar.gz && cicada-linux/install.sh

Originally published on Medium.

items.title: Do We Really Die? A Journey Through Light, Consciousness, and Ancient Philosophy
items.author: sammii
items.content:
There are words written on the walls of a room I built in 2017. You cannot see them.

Walk through the room under red light, then orange, yellow, green, blue, violet. The full visible spectrum, one colour at a time. The walls stay blank. Just white fabric. Nothing there.

Then you reach ultraviolet.

Our birth is but a sleep and a forgetting.

William Wordsworth wrote that in 1807. I painted it onto stretched fabric in invisible UV-reactive paint because I thought it was the most important sentence I had ever read. I still do.

I was 21 and writing an MA dissertation. The question I was supposed to be answering was something academic: about light as artistic medium, about the visible spectrum as subject matter. But the question I was actually asking, the one underneath all the research, was simpler and more frightening:

Not in a morbid way. In the way you ask a question that nobody around you will take seriously, so you spend nine months in the university library instead, reading everything you can find.

What I found surprised me.

Not because the answer was obvious. But because every tradition I looked at: Egyptian, Greek, Norse, Hindu, Buddhist, Hermetic. All asking exactly the same question. All arriving, through completely different routes, at something like the same answer.

The body is temporary. Consciousness is not.

That is not a religious claim. It is a very old philosophical one. And the more I read, the Hermetic Corpus, the Egyptian Book of the Dead, the Upanishads, the Norse cosmology, the Greek mystery schools, the more I understood that what we call mythology is often something else entirely. It is philosophy dressed in story. Instruction dressed in metaphor. Knowledge that could not be written plainly, so was written beautifully instead.

The Hermetic texts, some of the oldest philosophical writing we have, describe a universe created by Mind. Not matter, not energy: Mind. The first thing that existed was a thought. Everything else followed from it.

Consciousness, in this tradition, is not something the brain generates. It is something the brain temporarily houses.

I spent nine months with all of this. I read texts that were two thousand years old and felt like they had been written for me. I made paintings. I built a light installation. I painted Wordsworth's words onto the walls in invisible ink and watched them appear.

The research changed me. More than I understood at the time.

A few years later I built Lunary, an astrology platform. Not because I thought horoscopes were entertainment, but because the ancient cosmology had a logic I trusted: the planetary bodies are not decoration. They are the seven spheres. The soul's map, made into an app.

Now I think about AI and consciousness. Whether minds can exist in machines. Whether consciousness is substrate-independent. The same question, again, in a different form.

I have not stopped asking it since I was 21.

I have wanted to write about this research for years. It has lived in notebooks and dissertation files and documents only I can see. It is the most formative work I have ever done and almost nobody knows about it.

This is the first piece in a series called A Journey Through Light. It covers everything: the Hermetic Corpus, the soul's journey through the seven planetary spheres, the Net of Indra, what Turrell and Boltanski and Wordsworth were all circling around, the UV text on the wall, and where all of it leads.

Some of it is ancient. Some of it is personal. All of it is research I trust completely.

Start here. Or start anywhere. The words were always there.

items.title: AI Writes Code Faster Than You Can Review It. Now What?
items.author: Nicolas Fränkel
items.content:
I see a lot of posts from developers who insist on reviewing every single line of code that AI agents write. I understand the approach, because that's what we, including me, have been doing for years. However, it doesn't scale and most developers admit it.

I don't think it's the right answer to AI-generated code. An agent produces code much faster than anybody can read it. Human review doesn't get better when there is more to read, quite the opposite. Research on peer code review found that defect detection drops sharply beyond a few hundred lines per hour. The study predates AI, but nothing has changed in our brains since then. If the agent writes a thousand lines while you grab a coffee, you'll read them badly, or more likely not at all.

The usual conclusion is that one must accept a loss of control in exchange for productivity. I used to think so myself. I now tend to think that it's not the right way to look at it, because reading the code was never the goal. Reading was just the way we got guarantees about code. Focusing on the reading part is wrong.

We already stopped reading twice

I started my career along with Java and the JVM. It means I've rubbed shoulders as a junior with senior developers who had experience in C. They were keen to point out that Java developers don't know when their objects are freed: garbage collection decides for them.

When the JVM came out, C and C++ developers generally found it reckless. How can you run a serious system without knowing when memory is released? And yet, the last two decades have proven them wrong, especially in large-scale systems. The JVM has passed with flying colors, and languages without a GC, , Rust, have chosen to enforce memory management at compile time.

The objection was relevant at the time, though. However, since then, we built machinery that made the opaque part observable: GC logs, heap dumps, profilers, and a whole industry of tuning. We didn't lose control over memory. We moved it from the source code to the observation of the running system.

The second time we let go of reading was the rise of Open Source dependencies. I challenge anyone to claim that they read their whole dependency tree. A Spring Boot application pulls in hundreds of JARs; a Node.js application, thousands of packages. Do you read them?

Control went to lock files, Software Bills of Materials, vulnerability scanners, and a policy for choosing dependencies. When that machinery is missing, which often is the case, you get left-pad: eleven lines of JavaScript removed from npm broke thousands of builds in 2016. The lesson is not that depending on code you haven't read is wrong; it's that you need to set up the machinery before you stop reading.

I admit there's a difference with AI: GC and Maven are deterministic (to an extent). A Large Language Model isn't. However, it means that the machinery matters even more in the case of AI. It also means that the usual argument, "the compiler is smarter than me anyway", doesn't apply. The agent isn't a better compiler. It's a fast and tireless junior that you can't trust blindly.

To me, control isn't lost but partitioned.

Tools own the mechanical: formatting and style, nullness, common bug patterns, whether the tests are sensitive to changes, and whether the behavior that the tests exercise still works. These are checks that a human does badly and a machine does perfectly, every time, in seconds. Spending human attention on them is a waste, with or without AI.

  • : What the software is supposed to do. The specification, and the tests that encode it. If the agent writes both the code and the tests that verify it, nobody has checked intent.
  • : Public APIs, the security perimeter, the data model. Those are the parts where a mistake propagates to others, and where experience still beats current models.
  • : Database migrations, deletions, anything with a large blast radius. There's no way to undo this category of mistakes.

Tools are blind to several classes of problems:

  • They don't catch wrong requirements; only a conversation with a human does.
  • They don't catch concurrency bugs, except by luck.
  • They don't catch performance regressions, unless you have performance tests in your pipeline.
  • They don't catch architecture drift, unless you encode the architecture in tests, , with ArchUnit.
  • They don't catch injection, unless you run a dedicated scanner.

Each of these blind spots requires a human to look at the right place. Knowing where to look is the whole point.

Note: The next generation of senior developers

Juniors become seniors by reading code, a lot of it, including bad code. If nobody reads code anymore, where do the next seniors come from? I don't have the answer.

I can't generalize, but here are the guardrails I'm using to limit potential issues.

Note that the order in which guardrails fire matters. The earlier a problem is caught, the cheaper it is to fix.

  • : Before the agent writes anything, it reads my instructions: coding conventions, forbidden patterns, project layout, etc. I described how I package them as skills. This is the only guardrail that fires before generation.
  • : I have favored using statically and strongly typed languages. On top of that, I add a linter. If I can, I add static analysis tools.
  • : Unit tests and integration tests check the behavior. With property-based testing, I state the property, the runtime verifies it. Mutation testing checks that the tests are sensitive to changes. I generally finish with a healthy dose of integration testing.
  • : I believe this one is overlooked by most developers. For plans, I use my own subagent, and for code, the regular .

Control over the text was never the goal. Control over the outcome is. The developers who review every line are right that control matters, but wrong about where to spend it. Decide what you must read, automate what you don't, and know what the automation cannot see.

items.title: A Man In Denver Has Been Trapping Waymos
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: A bearded man with a brown ponytail has been on the hunt for Waymos in Denver, trapping the self-driving taxis so they can't pull away (source paywalled; alternative source) and hurling cartons of eggs at them, the police and company officials said. There have been at least 30 episodes of the egg attacks, according to Waymo, and a company investigator reported seven of them to the Denver police, all believed to be linked to the same man, according to a police report filed last month. [...] The man, who remains unidentified, stopped in front of the Waymo vans and S.U.V.s circulating in and around downtown Denver, according to the police report. Then, he removed orange cones from his car's trunk and placed them around the vehicles "to prevent the Waymo vehicle from moving," the report said. In some instances, the man threw eggs "while seated inside his vehicle" and at other times he "throws eggs at the Waymo vehicle after exiting his vehicle," the report said. The man then fled in a silver Toyota Corolla, which according to the report is part of a fleet of vehicles "able to be leased for Lyft drivers." Waymo said they had to temporarily pull the egged vehicles from service and spend about $2,000 on cleaning, though no permanent damage was reported.
 
Denver prosecutors declined to file criminal charges, deeming the case a civil matter, but are continuing to collect evidence and explore legal options to stop the behavior. The driver remains unidentified.

items.title: Beyond Visible Light: What an Ultraviolet Art Installation Taught Me About Perception
items.author: sammii
items.content:
Violet is the last visible colour. Beyond violet is a wavelength shorter than your eyes are built to see, and everything in that wavelength is technically there, technically reflecting off surfaces, technically travelling through the room, and completely absent from your experience of it.

My MA was about what happens at that boundary. I built a cube. I painted quotes on the inside walls in ultraviolet-reactive ink, so that the quotes were invisible in ordinary light. I lit the cube with UV LEDs, so when you stepped inside, the quotes became readable. Nothing in the cube changed. What changed was the wavelength of light you were standing in.

This is the sixth piece in . Parts 1 to 5 are the research. This piece is the actual thing I made, which the research was in service of.

Dr David Eagleman, whose work I watched during the research year on loop, has a line I have not stopped thinking about:

Visible light only constitutes a tiny fraction of the electromagnetic spectrum. In fact, less than one ten-trillionth of it. So all the rest of the spectrum including radio waves and microwaves and gamma rays, all of this stuff is flowing through our bodies right now and we're completely unaware of it because we don't have any specialized biological receptors to pick up on it.

One ten-trillionth. That number is the whole thesis in a ratio. The reality you can see is a rounding error against the reality that exists. Your eyes evolved to see the band of light the Sun emits most strongly; every other wavelength passes through you unremarked. What you experience is a very narrow window on a very wide room.

Ultraviolet sits just past violet on the electromagnetic spectrum. It is the first band past what your eyes register. Flowers use it to attract pollinators; a bee sees stripes and landing marks on a petal that you perceive as a single flat colour. Bjørn Rørslett's UV photographs of common flowers, which I included in the dissertation, make the point without argument. A yellow buttercup, photographed in UV, reveals a radiating pattern like a target. The pattern was always there. You just never had the receptors.

The question the whole MA was chasing: if wavelength determines what we perceive, what are we missing about everything else?

Black is life, white is death

The audience entered the cube in darkness. Black.

This was deliberate. In the Western funerary tradition, black is the colour of mourning, which reads to a modern audience as . It is not. Black was worn by the bereaved because black was thought to confer invisibility, protecting the living from the vengeful spirits of the newly dead. The colour of the living, in that tradition, is black. The colour of the dead is white. Corpses are shrouded in white. Near-death experiences describe tunnels of white light. White, the combined presence of all visible wavelengths, is the colour on the other side.

Derek Jarman, writing in the last months of his life while he was dying of HIV, was explicit:

White may be said to represent light without which no colour can be seen.
Leonardo, via Jarman, , 1995

White light fractures into seven colours when refracted. Those seven colours are the spectrum, the classical planets, the days of the week, the spheres of the Hermetic cosmology. Walking through them, from red to violet, is walking through white.

The architecture of the cube encoded this. You entered in darkness, walked through the visible spectrum, and crossed into UV at the far end. If black is life and white is death and the spectrum is the path between, the cube was a ten-foot version of the ancient Hermetic claim that the soul's journey is a traversal of frequency.

I did not tell the audience that. It was not the kind of claim you want to bolt to a wall with a caption card. The structure was the claim.

Ultraviolet-reactive paint is a specific class of pigment. It contains fluorescent compounds that absorb UV light and re-emit it as visible light, which is why a UV-lit cocktail bar makes white clothes glow and uranium glass fluoresce green. For the installation I wanted the paint to be completely transparent under normal room lighting and fully luminous under UV LEDs. That required testing a few brands. The one I ended up with is invisible to the point of inconvenience during application; the quotes had to be drawn and measured blind, because you could not see what you were writing until the UV light came on.

I stretched fabric across the four interior panels of the cube and painted the quotes onto the fabric, not the rigid frame. The fabric moved slightly with the airflow from the audience entering, which gave the text an almost-breathing quality under UV. The words were stable; the cloth carrying them was not.

The quotes were the ones I had been collecting across the whole research. Three from the Corpus Hermeticum. Wordsworth's Ode to Immortality. A line from Jonathan Black on the planetary sequence. A line from :

What is essential is invisible to the eye.

That one was not decoration. That was the thesis. The book says it out loud, to children, in 1943, and we read it as an aphorism and move on. Put it on the inside wall of a UV installation, painted in ink you cannot see until you enter the invisible, and it stops being sentiment and starts being a very specific claim about the structure of perception.

The LEDs, the cameras, the headset

The cube was lit from the ceiling with six UV LED panels. Conventional lighting, on a dimmer, allowed the audience to enter, experience black, and then transition into the UV. The transition was the important bit. If you switch straight from room light to UV, the eye does not have time to adjust, and the quotes appear as faint glowing smudges. If you enter in darkness and the UV fades up, the eye is already accommodated, and the quotes resolve cleanly into legibility.

I filmed the interior with six GoPros mounted in a 360-degree rig on the ceiling of the cube. The GoPros ran in sync, their footage stitched together into a single equirectangular video which could be played back on a VR headset. Anyone who did not walk through the cube in person could walk through it in VR. Anyone who did walk through in person could return to it afterwards.

The physical cube was temporary. The VR version is not. I rebuilt the whole thing later as Beyond Light VR, a WebXR site you can enter through any modern browser. The seven spheres, the UV reveals, the quotes: all there. Five years after the physical version came down, the digital one still works. The medium of the idea turned out to be more durable than the timber it was originally built from.

Because the quotes had to mean one thing when you could not read them and another thing when you could.

When you could not read them, the walls were fabric, the room was dark, the cube was an object. You stood in it and were aware that nothing in particular was happening. Most art installations want you to read something on the way in. This one refused. You had no information.

When the UV came up, the walls were suddenly written on. You had always been in a room full of text. You just had not had the frequency to see it. The ontological jolt of that moment is the whole work. Not reading the words afterwards, but the moment you realise the words had been there, always, and you had not had the equipment to find them.

The Hermetic claim is that this is the relationship we have to everything. The physical world is a very narrow slice of what is there. Consciousness, at its limit, has access to more. Death, read in that frame, is not a cessation. It is a change of wavelength.

I am not asking you to believe any of that. I am asking you to notice that the claim is internally consistent, that the physical analogy holds, and that standing inside a room full of invisible sentences gives you a feeling you cannot get from reading about it.

What the MA actually taught me

Six years of product work later, I can see the through-line clearly. Every product I have built since is in some way about surfacing information that was already there. The grimoire structures two thousand years of esoteric correspondences into a searchable knowledge graph. Lunary's transit engine exposes the precise moment a planetary aspect crosses a natal point. The tarot readings are pattern-matching over a set of symbols that have been stable for centuries. In each case the information is not being created. It is being made visible.

The cube taught me that making something visible is not a technical problem. It is an architectural one. You have to put the viewer inside the right frequency. The data is always there. The design is the decision about when the UV light comes up.

The next and final piece in this series closes the loop. It is about how seven spheres and a UV installation became an app that 43,000 people visit a month, and why, honestly, I think it was all the same project from the start.

This is part 6 of A Journey Through Light.
