Ask any AI shopping agent to find the best price and it will happily return one. The harder question is whether that price is for the same thing. A vacuum listed at two stores can differ by model year, bundle or pack size, and a price comparison that misses that is worse than none at all.

Deal.ai, an AI shopping agent built by Famous Labs, has been measuring both problems: how much prices really differ for identical products, and how hard it is to know two listings are identical in the first place.

The results were consistent. About two in three products had prices at least 5% apart across the big retailers. Among the 4,684 products sold at four or more retailers, a shopper who checked one store picked at random paid, on average, 15.6% above the lowest listed price. Checking two stores cut that to 7.4%, three stores to 3.7%, and four to 1.1%.

The hard part: matching the product

Those numbers only mean something if every price is for the same item. Deal.ai's answer is to separate matching from pricing.

In a live recheck on November 5, Deal.ai drew 600 products at random and kept the ones with a brand and a model number or barcode. A separate AI model then read each store's own listing title, with prices hidden, and kept only listings that were the identical item: same model, size, capacity, pack count and generation. Colour could differ; bundles, refurbished and open-box listings could not.

Of 4,990 store listings, 1,886 passed. That is a strict filter by design. It throws away near-matches that a looser system would happily compare, which keeps a "lower price" from really being a smaller pack or last year's model. Hiding prices from the matching model matters too: it stops the model from being swayed toward a match by a price that looks plausible.

"Finding prices is the easy part. The hard part is making sure every store is selling the exact same product, the same model and the same size," said Alex Mehr, Ph.D., co-founder and CEO of Famous Labs, the company behind Deal.ai. "That's what our agents are built to check, so shoppers can trust the price comparison they see."

Deal.ai puts that work behind a simple interface. Shoppers ask for what they want in plain English, and the agent researches the options, compares live prices across thousands of stores and sends them to the store with the best deal. Its agents also run every hour to surface unusually good deals, each with a deal score out of 10. A free deal checker takes a link to any deal and finds the same item at every big store.

For developers, Deal.ai also offers an MCP server, so other AI assistants can call it directly instead of scraping stores themselves.

Price data is abundant. Trustworthy comparisons are not. The gap between one store and the best price is large enough to matter to shoppers, but only if the agent is honest about which listings truly match. Strict matching, with prices hidden from the matcher, is a simple rule that makes every number after it more believable.

Deal.ai is free at deal.ai. The full study is published on Deal.ai's research page.

items.title: Your AI Is Generating PRs, Not ROI
items.author: PlayerZero
items.content:
AI coding tools are generating more pull requests than ever, but more PRs don't equal ROI unless that code ships, holds up in production and reduces work downstream.

Ask any engineering leader if their team uses AI to write code, and you'll get a yes before you finish the question. Ask them what that AI is worth, and watch the yes turn into a pause.

That pause is the actual state of the industry right now. Not "should we adopt AI." That question is over. The question nobody has a good answer to is simpler and more uncomfortable: can you prove it worked?

We talk to a lot of engineering leaders whose teams have already bought the AI. Vendors, internal agents, standardized copilots, all of it. And when we ask how they know it's paying off, we hear some version of the same three things, over and over, from companies that have nothing else in common.

Here's the accepted story: AI writes code faster, so engineering gets faster, so the org gets more done. It's clean. It's also wrong, or at least wrong enough to be dangerous.

Speed of code generation isn't the same thing as speed of value delivery. We've heard this described, almost word for word, by leaders at very different companies: their AI tooling is optimized for the speed of the coding loop, and that optimization is flooding review queues with pull requests that don't address the problems actually costing them money. One technology leader we spoke with put a number on it: their organization still allocates 30 to 40 percent of R&D to legacy sustenance. An AI that makes commits faster doesn't touch that number. It might make it worse, because now there's more code to sustain.

More code, faster, is a vanity metric. It looks like progress on a dashboard. It is not the same thing as fewer defects, fewer escalations, less tech debt, or a codebase anyone actually trusts. If your only instrumented signal is "how fast did we ship the diff," you've measured the part of the SDLC that was never the bottleneck.

You built the agents. Can you prove they work?

The more sophisticated a team gets with AI, the worse this problem gets, not better. We talked with a leader at an enterprise planning-software company who had built dozens of finance agents and an internal factory that turns specs directly into agents. Real infrastructure, real investment. And their honest assessment was that they have no standardized way to measure how their engineers actually use these tools, and now they're dealing with agent sprawl: agents triggering each other, versioning headaches, token spend nobody forecasted, and a growing need to gate daisy-chained agents just to protect the budget and the systems underneath them. This team caps R&D spend as a percentage of revenue and wants AI to bring that number down every year. Nobody can currently tell them if it is.

That's not a failure of ambition. It's a failure of measurement discipline arriving after the infrastructure, instead of before it.

We heard the same shape of problem from a team running a home-grown AI development process, stitched together across a project tracker, a code host, an LLM, and a browser-automation tool for execution. It works, in the sense that a demo works. But their own words to me were that the current evaluation criteria are largely subjective, and what they actually want is a clean, quantifiable way to tell the business whether the tooling is worth what it costs. A demo is not a metric. A vibe is not ROI.

The "we already have an AI" wall

There's a second version of this problem that shows up earlier in the buying process. Teams benchmark every new AI purchase against the general-purpose AI they already pay for. We've had conversations where the honest pushback was some version of: our senior engineers already get most of what they need from existing docs and the chat assistant they use every day, so why would we pay for something else? That's a fair question, and it's one every vendor in this category, including us, has to answer with evidence, not adjectives.

None of this is a story about bad tools. Cursor-style coding assistants, general chat assistants, internal agent factories: they're all doing exactly what they were built to do, which is help someone write code faster. The gap isn't in the tool. It's in the fact that "wrote code faster" was never the metric that mattered, and almost nobody instrumented the metric that does.

What actually counts as ROI

If speed of code generation is the wrong number, what's the right one? It's the same handful of things it's always been, just harder to see once agents are shipping code faster than anyone can review it by hand: defects that never reach production. Tickets that never escalate to L3. Tech debt that shrinks instead of compounding. Time to root cause. Time to trust a change before it ships.

Those aren't vibes. They're measurable — but only by something that holds your code, your production behavior, and what your customers actually report in one model instead of three disconnected tools. That's the argument for an engineering world model: not more code, but a traceable line from every change to its consequence, and the judgment to tell you which one you're looking at. Code simulations exist for the same reason: catching the defect before it merges is worth more than shipping the diff a day earlier. Agentic debugging is worth more than agentic writing, because writing was never the expensive part of the SDLC. Understanding what you wrote always was.

The teams we talked with weren't wrong to adopt AI. They were wrong about which loop to speed up. Every engineering org we know is currently running an experiment on itself, at scale, with no control group and no instrumentation. Fix the instrumentation before you fix the model. The PRs were never the point.

Want to see how much engineering capacity your team could recover with a multiplayer platform? Run your numbers with PlayerZero's AI ROI calculator.

items.title: SpaceX Wins FCC Approval To Deploy 1 Million Orbital Data Center Satellites
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has authorized SpaceX to deploy one million AI computing satellites into orbit as part of its solar-powered Starmind data center constellation. The approval comes despite opposition from Amazon, Viasat and the American Astronomical Society. CNBC reports: The FCC, in its authorization filing (PDF), noted that SpaceX's application "received a substantial number of comments from the public, including petitions to deny filed by Kuiper Systems LLC (Amazon Leo), Viasat Inc. (Viasat), and the American Astronomical Society (AAS)." In a March petition urging the FCC to deny SpaceX's application, Amazon had labeled the company's Starmind project as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan."
 
The e-commerce and cloud computing giant is building a competitor to SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, and said it would take SpaceX "centuries" to build the constellation, adding that the company provided scant details about how it would "deliver on these grand claims." The petition resulted in a rebuke from [FCC Chairman Brendan Carr], who said Amazon "should focus on the fact" that it's falling short of its own satellite deployment milestone. In a post on X, Carr said SpaceX's Starmind constellation and "competitor constellations will use solar power to extend America's lead in Super Intelligence."
 
Musk said in a reply, "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."

items.title: Who Was Hermes Trismegistus, and Why Does He Still Matter?
items.author: sammii
items.content:
Every path in my MA led back to one figure, and the figure was not historical.

The Corpus Hermeticum, the sub-lunar sphere, the seven planetary spheres, the idea that nothing dies but dissolves and recombines, the claim that the cosmos was thought into being before it was made. All of it is attributed to a man called Hermes Trismegistus. Hermes Thrice-Greatest. And when you try to find the man, he is not there.

Who he was, depending on who you ask

There are three different answers to the question of who Hermes Trismegistus was, and all three were taken seriously at different points in history.

The first answer is that he was a real Egyptian sage, a contemporary or near-contemporary of Moses, who wrote down the wisdom of the gods. This is what Renaissance humanists believed when they rediscovered the texts in the fifteenth century. Marsilio Ficino translated the Corpus Hermeticum into Latin in 1463 for Cosimo de' Medici, interrupting his translation of Plato because his patron thought the Hermetica was older and therefore more important. Cosimo turned out to be wrong about the dating. The Hermetica ended up shaping Renaissance thought anyway.

The second answer is that he was a later composite, a syncretic figure that emerged when Greek and Egyptian religion fused in Alexandria. The Greek god Hermes, messenger and guide of souls, was identified with the Egyptian god Thoth, scribe of the gods and inventor of writing. Thrice-Greatest is a title that belongs to Thoth in earlier Egyptian texts. The merging happened somewhere between the founding of Alexandria in 331 BCE and the collation of the surviving Hermetic corpus in the second and third centuries CE. No single person wrote the Corpus Hermeticum. A tradition wrote it, over generations, under one name.

The third answer is the one the texts themselves give. The Hermetica presents Hermes not as a historical person at all, but as a stand-in for divine intelligence writing through human hands. In that reading the question of who wrote it is the wrong question. The point is that the ideas are not the property of any individual.

The first answer is wrong. The second is almost certainly correct. The third is the one the texts insist on.

What the Corpus Hermeticum actually is

Eighteen books, of which seventeen survive. Book Fifteen is lost. The surviving texts were collated in Alexandria in the second and third centuries CE, written in Greek, Latin and Coptic. Not in the hieroglyphs you might expect of something claiming Egyptian origin. The translation into English I worked from most often was John Everard's 1650 version, which has an archaic cadence you can almost hear when you read it out loud:

I am gone out of myself into an immortal body, and am not now, what I was before, but was begotten in Mind.

Atum is the central figure of the cosmology. Atum is the cosmic mind, the pre-existing intelligence that contains all potential. The word itself is older than the Hermetic texts; it belongs to ancient Egyptian religion, where Atum was the self-created god of Heliopolis. The Hermetic writers inherit the name and keep most of its original meaning. Atum is the first thing that existed. Atum is the totality of everything that exists. Atum is not a person.

From Atum comes everything, through thought. The physical universe is not primary. Matter is not the foundation. Thought is the foundation, and matter is what thought produces when it slows down enough to become form. This is what the Hermetic phrase light precipitates matter actually means. Light, in the Hermetic sense, is not photons. It is the intelligence of the cosmos, from which matter crystallises as the expression of thought taking shape.

Why the Thoth-Hermes synthesis matters

Thoth was the Egyptian god of writing, wisdom, measurement, time, and the moon. He mediated between worlds and wrote the words of magic that structured reality. Hermes was the Greek god of crossings, boundaries, messages, and guides. is the one who escorts souls across the threshold of death.

When the two merged, what emerged was a figure who was simultaneously the source of all written knowledge and the guide across the threshold of death. This is not a small coincidence. The Hermetic corpus is fundamentally about crossings: between the known and the unknowable, the living and the dead, the material and the immaterial. The figure who authored it had to be able to stand in both worlds at once.

Mead, in his 1906 translation, put it precisely:

Thus Thoth is especially the representative of the Spirit, the Inner Reason of all things; he is the Protector of all earthly laws, and every regulation of human society.

That phrase is the whole thing. The claim embedded in the Thoth-Hermes synthesis is that the same intelligence which governs the structure of the cosmos also governs the structure of law, language, measurement, and thought. The writer of the universe is the writer of grammar.

The Hermetica is explicit that death is not what it appears to be.

For there is nothing dead, that either hath been, or is, or shall be in the World. For they do not die, O Son, but as Compound bodies they are dissolved. But dissolution is not death; and they are dissolved, not that they may be destroyed, but that they may be made new.

Read slowly. Dissolution is not death. The physical form disperses. The arrangement of matter changes. But nothing that was there is gone, because the matter itself was only a temporary form. What survives is what was always primary: the thought, the pattern, the intelligence that gathered the matter into a shape in the first place.

This is not a religious claim about an afterlife. It is a cosmological claim about what kind of thing a thing is. For the Hermetic writers, everything in the physical world is a local, temporary expression of a thought in Atum's mind. When the local form dissipates, the thought does not. The universe is not made of objects. It is made of acts of thinking, with objects as their residue.

I built a cube. I painted quotes on its fabric walls in ultraviolet paint. I lit it with LEDs. I filmed the inside with six GoPros to make a 360-degree video you could enter through a VR headset. The whole project was an argument that reality depends on what you can perceive, and that what you can perceive is a tiny fraction of what exists.

The Corpus Hermeticum says the same thing, earlier and more seriously. The visible spectrum is one sliver of electromagnetic radiation. The physical body is one expression of consciousness. The seven classical planets are one layer of a cosmological system that keeps going beyond them. In every direction, the Hermetica says: what you can see is evidence of something larger that you cannot.

Hermes Trismegistus is the name we put on the claim that the larger thing is legible. That reality is not only accessible to the senses, which know very little, but to the mind, which can read the structure of the cosmos the way a scribe reads a scroll. That the universe is authored, not accidental. Whether or not you accept the claim, the claim itself is the foundation of every Western esoteric tradition that follows. Neoplatonism inherits it. The Renaissance inherits it. Jung inherits it. Most of what we now call symbolic or archetypal thinking traces back, eventually, to a nobody called Thrice-Greatest writing under an Egyptian name in a Greek city.

I did not come out of the MA believing Hermes Trismegistus was real in the way that Moses was. I came out of it believing he was real in the way that Sherlock Holmes is real. He is the voice through which a particular way of reading the cosmos was kept alive for two thousand years, across cultures and languages, intact enough that an undergraduate could find him in a library and understand him.

The next piece in this series looks at what that cosmology actually says about mythology: the planetary gods, the Saturn-Jupiter lineage, and why Greek myth reads differently once you know it is cosmological instruction in disguise.

This is part 4 of A Journey Through Light.

items.title: How a Side-Channel Attack Exposed Hidden Data in OpenSearch
items.author: Kevin Hwang
items.content:
In our research, we found an unauthorized data access vulnerability in OpenSearch that allowed an attacker to extract vector fields protected by field-level security using OpenSearch's vector search as a side-channel.

We reported the issue to OpenSearch team along with a proposed patch, and the vulnerability has since been fixed as of 3.10.

OpenSearch is an open source distributed search engine created by Amazon, a popular alternative proprietary Elasticsearch.

Besides the more traditional lexical search and analytics capabilities, it also functions as a vector database, which has become increasingly important for AI and ML applications — RAG, semantic search, recommender systems, etc.

One of the most common use cases of vector databases is to store and search for .

An embedding is a point or vector that represents some concept — e.g., a word, image, or something more abstract and opaque — in some high dimensional embedding space.

Often in these embedding spaces, spatial relationships encode semantic relationships. E.g., in the example below:

  • "King" is close to "prince," but far from, say, "computer"
  • Going from "king" to "queen" is to going from "man" to "woman"

Tl;dr, vector databases are important, and OpenSearch is one such popular database technology.

OpenSearch has a security feature called field-level security (FLS) which allows you to control which document fields a role can read in an index.

For example, a cluster might have users with different roles, e.g., QA, support, MLEs, SREs accessing the cluster for different purposes, along with service principals representing different programatic workloads — documents might be composed of different data that not all should have access to even when they have access to an underlying document itself.

FLS essentially allows you to create different projections of an index with different fields visible or hidden to different users, without having to duplicate that data into a separate index per view.

A wild side-channel appears!

In using FLS, we noticed something intriguing: while FLS the literal values of fields from users for whom that field was configured as excluded, and while those fields were completely disregarded by lexical search, if the field was a vector field, it was still eligible for vector search, and still influenced search candidacy, scoring, and ranking.

If you're familiar with the idea of side-channels in security, alarm bells should be going off in your head right now. 🚨

The Art Of The Side-Channel

Any time you have an inaccessible secret, but you are able to indirectly learn information correlated with it, you have a potential side-channel vulnerability.

  • In 2004, researchers demonstrated microphone recordings of a computer performing cryptographic RSA operations could be used to recover the private key. As the CPU worked, power consumption varied, along with timing of different steps in the workflow, which caused variations in the noise emitted by different electrical components, apparently enough to work out the data the CPU was operating on.
  • In 2023, researchers demonstrated an attack where a video recording taken by a smartphone camera of another device's status LED while it was performing cryptographic operations could be used to recover private keys. In their own words:

The intensity/color of the power LEDs can be used to detect the beginning and end of cryptographic operations. This can be done because the intensity/brightness of a device's power LED […] correlates with its power consumption (which is affected by the CPU operations). This is caused by the fact that the power LED is connected directly to the power line of the electrical circuit which lacks effective means (e.g., filters, voltage stabilizers) of decoupling the correlation with the power consumption.

The OpenSearch FLS k-NN Attack

Here's how the attack works:

At a high level, if a document with a hidden vector field can be included and scored in a vector search, the score returned for a particular query vector will be some measure of the similarity between and . With clever probing of , we can reconstruct .

For example, for an L2 vector space, OpenSearch documents the distance function between two vectors as the squared Euclidean distance.

For a given hidden vector and query vector (the probe), this gives us:

The squared distance is thus recoverable from the score:

Then, for a unit basis vector :

From which the components of can be computed:

For an n-dimensional vector, this requires n+1 probes to recover the original .

This still requires that the target document enter the k-NN candidate set — in order to return a score — for each probe query. In theory this may be difficult if the index is large and there are many vectors, but in practice this can often be achieved, and an attacker can increase their chances by upping the k of the query.

Let's walk through an example.

There's a document in you have access to with:

  • A 2-D vector field whose value (say, ) is hidden to you due to FLS exclusions
  • Visible fields like

You send 3 search queries:

GET /index_1/_search
{
  "size": 1,
  "query": {
    "bool": {
      "must": [{ "knn": { "hidden_vec": { "vector": [0, 0], "k": 128 } } }],
      "filter": [{ "term": { "visible_tag": "target" } }]
    }
  }
}

Repeat twice more with and . OpenSearch returns the following s, from which the squared distances can be computed from the derivations above:

Substituting these into the equations above yields , approximately (due to the scores being rounded) the original vector in this case!

Voilà, you've just stolen a vector via side-channel! 🎉

The technical root cause was a flaw in the k-NN plugin's implementation of vector search: unlike lexical search which completely disregards FLS-excluded fields for purposes of matching and ranking via filtered view, the k-NN plugin during vector search unwrapped the filtered view, accessing the raw reader underneath and thus considered as candidates vectors that should've been hidden by FLS, and returned their scores.

Coordinated Disclosure Timeline

  • Vulnerability discovered, reported
  • OpenSearch SRT accepted report
  • Fix scheduled for OpenSearch 3.10.0
  • OpenSearch 3.10.0 released

items.title: 6 Ways to Disagree With Someone Without Damaging the Relationship
items.author: Vinita Bansal
items.content:
Most of us find it hard to speak up at work and it gets even more challenging when we aren’t just sharing an idea, but refuting someone else’s viewpoint. Becoming too eager to tell others they’re wrong can invite pushback and make others dismiss or disregard your thinking. Attacking their intelligence or motives, acting mean or belittling them in any way can put them on the defensive and kill any chance you had to find a better solution. When others feel judged, misunderstood or unsupported, they feel unsafe which makes them more cautious, watchful and guarded. Instead of handling the disagreement with openness and curiosity, they try to protect themselves by retaliating, arguing or becoming disengaged.

Keeping quiet and not speaking up is also not an option because holding your thoughts and not sharing them can lead to bad choices and poor decisions. It can result in missed opportunities, mediocre solutions and terrible mistakes. Not contributing to the discussion with the fear of how it will be perceived or worrying about damaging the relationship keeps you safe, but it also prevents you from embracing discomfort, which is necessary for growth.

Disagreeing with others in a way that does not increase tension, make the other person feel attacked, criticized or lead to defensive and argumentative behavior requires kind clarity—being direct and honest while maintaining empathy and . It requires delivering honest opinions without sugar-coating, while ensuring they feel respected and valued. It requires challenging them while continuing to be supportive.

People often silence themselves, or "agree to disagree" without fully exploring the actual nature of the disagreement, for the sake of protecting a relationship and maintaining connection. But when we avoid certain conversations, and never fully learn how the other person feels about all of the issues, we sometimes end up making assumptions that not only perpetuate but deepen misunderstandings, and that can generate resentment.

Follow these practices to show maturity by disagreeing with others without being disrespectful.

Listen before you speak, show you value their opinion

When you find a flaw in someone’s argument, notice their mistake or have better suggestions on how something must be done, you may be tempted to interrupt and insert your opinion. But speaking up and disagreeing before giving an opportunity to another person to complete their thoughts or making them feel heard and understood leaves them feeling frustrated, doubted and attacked. Their instant reaction is to oppose, resist and fight back without evaluating your idea or suggestion.

Listening on the other hand, without expressing your disapproval in either words or body language, makes others feel trusted and respected. It creates an environment of psychological safety, clarifies your intent and sets the tone of the conversation that you’re not there to judge, impose or make them feel inferior.

  1. Pay attention to the non-verbal communication—tone of voice, hand gestures and body language. Your words convey your message, but your body language conveys feelings and emotions behind it. Nodding to show you’re listening to them while expressing disapproval in body language can turn others off.
  2. Acknowledge their feelings and point of view. Acknowledging does not mean that you agree with them. It simply means that you understand how they feel. For example you can say: “From what you’ve told me, I understand that you’re more inclined towards option A because...” “I see you are getting really stressed about…” “If I’m understanding you correctly, you are mad right now for ….”
  3. Don’t interrupt or appear impatient to get your message across. Stay calm and neutral.

Genuine listening means suspending memory, desire, and judgement and, for a few moments at least, existing for the other person.

When you speak to someone you disagree with, recognize their ideas and feelings first—show that what they have to say matters.

Don’t use emotive language or loaded words

Words used to convey disagreement plays a crucial role in how your message is perceived—whether others are receptive to your viewpoint or they outrightly reject it. Using words that come across as  judgmental or too opinionated or using language that’s disrespectful or sarcastic makes disagreement less about finding the best path forward and more about ego—protecting one’s self-respect and self-esteem. Offending others by passing personal remarks or trying to prove they’re wrong activates their amygdala, which triggers fight-flight-freeze response, turning an already difficult situation into an impossible one.

Avoiding words that have the potential to be misinterpreted, stating your views without making it personal or coming across too strong and expressing your concerns in a non-judgmental neutral tone can invite others to take your opinion seriously. They may engage with you to better understand your perspective, show curiosity to dig deeper and think more clearly, leading to a highly constructive discussion.

When sharing your disagreement, using certain words is a big no-no. They trigger intense negative feelings which puts others on the defensive:

  1. Generalizing words like “always” and “never.”
  2. Enforcing words like can’t, shouldn’t, must, have to.
  3. Words that challenge their character like bad, useless, worthless, inferior.
  4. Passing judgment with words like mistake, failure, unacceptable.

We cannot control the way people interpret our ideas or thoughts, but we can control the words and tones we choose to convey them. Peace is built on understanding, and wars are built on misunderstandings. Never underestimate the power of a single word, and never recklessly throw around words.

When you speak to someone you disagree with, think carefully about the effect of what you say and avoid emotionally charged words which makes the conversation ineffective.

Use questions to guide the conversation instead of jumping to conclusions

When you don’t agree with someone or have a different point of view, you may rush with an opinion, jump to conclusions or become impatient to get yourself heard. Being too direct can make you come across as pushy, rude, inconsiderate, insensitive and controlling. Directly stating your opinion without taking the time to understand their thinking—what are their beliefs, what matters to them, how did they reach this decision—can make you try very hard to get yourself heard, but your voice will never reach or get across to them.

Questioning, on the other hand, not only gets you closer to their perspective, it makes others feel valued and respected. When you show curiosity to understand others, they reciprocate in kind—your inputs don’t invite pushback, but are treated as an opportunity to explore, test and learn. Questions unlock thinking, gets you closer to differences of opinion and challenges you to reconsider your own point of view without considering it as the only option worthy of time and attention.

Seek clarity and invite others to talk by asking open ended questions:

  1. What do you think about …
  2. I would like to understand where you are coming from …
  3. Can you share a little more about how you see things …?

Questioning helps people gain perspective and understand the perspectives of others. As they see issues and problems from different points of view, they gain an appreciation for their complexity—and also expand the range of possible solutions.

When you speak to someone you disagree with, use questions to find common ground, uncover patterns and help others see the gaps in their thinking instead of stating it explicitly.

Try to influence their decision, not to change their mind

When you don’t agree with someone, you may feel compelled to change their mind by imposing your thoughts and trying to micromanage the outcome. You may attack their thoughts and beliefs, present strong evidence to prove they’re wrong and push aggressively to make them see the issue differently. Trying to change someone’s mind is a cognitive shift—years of ingrained beliefs and attitudes are hard to change because they’re tied to identity, ego and biases, making others “dig in” rather than change. When people feel their beliefs are being attacked, the conversation shifts from problem-solving to winning. The more you push, the more fixed those beliefs can become. Trying to change someone’s mind can also come across as corrective—they may feel you don’t respect their thinking, trust their judgment or that your perspective matters more than their point of view.

Trying to influence others on the other hand, is a behavioral shift—it involves discussing actions, priorities, risks, incentives or trade-offs to help others make a better decision in the moment regardless of their original belief. Influence is achieved through framing—What are the trade-offs? What are the second-order effects? What happens if we do nothing? The idea is to guide their thinking, not impose yours.

To influence someone you disagree with:

  1. Slow down and reflect: What matters to them in this decision? What outcome are they trying to protect? What would make this feel safe for them? What are they optimizing for? What risk are they trying to avoid? What constraints are they managing? What identity or reputation is at stake?
  2. Align interests by connecting your opinion to their priorities.
  3. Frame your suggestions as choices, not conclusions.
  4. Suggest incremental movements like running a small pilot, phased approach or some experiments instead of a full reversal of their method.

The key word in our definition of a disagreement (an unacceptable difference between two perspectives), isn’t “difference.” It’s “unacceptable.” Once the clash between perspectives becomes unacceptable, our motivation shifts from understanding minds to changing them, and from that shift springs a world of trouble.

When you speak to someone you disagree with, focusing on changing their mind can make you less influential as they feel managed and intellectually overpowered. Rather, explore together, invite reflection and try to expand their perspective instead of changing their belief.

Keep the conversation on track by reiterating over the end goal

Disagreements often turn unproductive and spiral out of control when conversations go off-track and lose focus. Finger-pointing, blame games and other irrelevant points of discussion divert attention away from the main goal. Giving in and contributing to these by sharing your own frustrations, disappointment or other concerns can waste everyone’s time and energy while not taking you any closer to your goals. Participating in unrelated topics or disconnected arguments derails you from discussing the main idea and making progress on reaching a mutual conclusion.

Remaining present and calm during the emotional moments, reminding everyone of the end goal and tactfully bringing the conversation back to the agenda can unlock clearer thinking, more rational arguments and a better aligned decision. It can pave the path to disagree and commit—disagree and commit divulges the importance of commitment despite our differences. At its core, it supports unity, maturity to disconnect our identity from our ideas and support others even when we do not agree with their point of view. It doesn’t hide the fact that we disagree nor dismiss the value of our opinion, it simply guides us to know when it’s time to get past our convictions and work with others instead of working against them. Reiterating the end goal recenters the discussion on shared purpose instead of competing opinions.

To keep the discussion on track:

  1. Call out the shared outcome explicitly. Shift from to a common objective.
  2. Clarify you agree on the destination, even if you disagree on the path to get there.
  3. Evaluate options by asking which path best serves the agreed outcome.
  4. If emotions arise, anchor back to purpose rather than pushing harder on your argument.

Respect for the problem places all that we're struggling with into the landscape of the conversation itself. It lets us step back and take a satellite view of the way our tough conversation is playing out. The conversation is no longer a battlefield, but a course of obstacles through which we move.

When you speak to someone you disagree with, discuss what’s relevant to the current conversation. Stay on track. Avoid going off-topic.

Walk away if it isn’t worth it

Some disagreements may never get resolved, not because you’re doing something wrong or you’re being unreasonable. However, despite your best efforts you may not be able to influence others or reach a conclusion. In some cases, disagreeing with someone superior to you or those in positions of power can even backfire—they may hold it against you which can impact your career and growth. People who display extreme insecurity, stubbornness, egotism or narcissism are often hard to disagree with because they do not want a productive conversation—they want to feel superior, in control and right. They will portray you as a difficult person to discredit your viewpoint. They enjoy arguing for the sake of winning and always take the opposite side regardless of what you say. They consider themselves as the smartest person in the room and belittle you to assert their superiority.

When disagreement feels like a battle or starts to impact your mental health and personal well-being, it’s wise to emotionally detach yourself and walk away from it. Nothing in this world is worth your sanity. It’s important to voice your opinion and share your thoughts, but when the conversation crosses the safe boundary and enters into an unhealthy zone, staying in it or letting yourself be bothered about it is a foolish thing to do. about it or spending more time and energy into fixing the situation may only make it harder to let it go.

To identify if you should walk away from a disagreement:

  1. If the decision doesn’t meaningfully impact you, it may not be worth your energy.
  2. If disagreeing further could damage your position without influencing the outcome, it’s wise to stay away.
  3. If the emotions are escalating and the discussion is becoming more reactive with each exchange, continuing the conversation might do more damage than good.
  4. If the other person isn’t interested in solving the problem, only in proving themselves right, it’s not worth continuing.
  5. If they interrupt you constantly, dismiss your thoughts without even considering or attack your character, respectfully disengage.

Reason tells us that we should always be able to work things out with words. But the absurdly profound truth is that in many crucial moments of conflict, when sanity and safety hang in the balance, choosing not to engage verbally can be by far the most powerful form of speech.

Not all disagreements need to be resolved and not all of them are worthy. Knowing the difference is crucial to be effective without losing your mind.

  1. When you don’t pay attention to others and show eagerness to disagree, you invite pushback, resistance and defensiveness. Adopting an attitude of listening encourages others to consider your viewpoint as they feel heard and understood.
  2. How you convey your thoughts matter more than your opinion. Using emotionally charged words, passing personal remarks or using a judgmental tone can trigger intense negative feelings in others. Be calm and respectful. Use words that are less likely to be misinterpreted or evoke strong reactions.
  3. Your viewpoint comes across as imposing when it’s stated as a conclusion instead of an idea that might be worthy of consideration. By asking questions, you can help others see the flaw in their thinking and guide them towards an alternate perspective without coming across as pushy, insensitive or controlling.
  4. Trying to fix people’s mind is futile—years of ingrained beliefs can’t be changed in a day. A more effective strategy is to influence their thinking by discussing actions, risks and priorities that are important to make an effective decision in the moment, regardless of what they believe.
  5. Conversations, especially the ones that involve differences of opinion, often derail from the original goal and lose focus by wasting time on inconsequential topics. By reminding people of the original objective and bringing the main agenda into focus, you can keep the discussion productive.
  6. You don’t need to resolve all disagreements, especially the ones that don’t directly impact you or the ones that compromise your sanity and peace of mind. Let them go, don’t bother yourself with the end outcome.

Introduction: Stop Renting Your Intelligence

Your AI bill doubled last quarter.

Your provider changed its usage caps again.

Your legal team will not let customer data touch a third-party API.

Your best engineer hit a rate limit in the middle of a production incident.

Most CTOs, founders and serious AI users have lived at least one of these lines this year.

That is why it’s high time every enterprise worldwide tool Local AI seriously.

Open-weight models crossed a threshold in 2026.

Kimi K3.1 Pro, GLM-5.3, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Muse Spark Open and Mistral Large 4 now trade blows with the closed frontier, and every one of them can be downloaded today.

Put the right model on the right hardware, and the token meter simply stops running.

This guide ranks 20 open-weight models in two Top Ten lists.

The first list is for enterprises running four 512 GB Mac Studios joined over Thunderbolt 5 into a 2,048 GB pool of unified memory.

The second is for power users with a single machine and at least 64 GB of VRAM or unified memory.

You will get parameter counts, architectures, published benchmarks, quantized and uncensored Hugging Face releases, a full quantization primer, two detailed budgets, and the security case for running all of this yourself.

If you are interested in Local LLMs, and saving your API bills (or eliminating them entirely) you need to read this!

Why Local AI Means Unlimited AI

Cloud AI is priced like electricity from a landlord.

You pay per token, you accept the landlord's rules, and the landlord can change the price whenever it likes.

Local AI turns that per-token bill into a capacity bill you own.

You pay once for hardware, then a modest amount for power, and the marginal cost of the next million tokens is close to zero.

Here is what changes the day your model runs on your own silicon:

  • - run agents overnight, re-run evaluations a hundred times, let a coding agent burn through a million tokens on a refactor - piece of cake.
  • - your only ceiling is the memory bandwidth of your machine.

Understanding Quantization

You cannot talk about local AI without talking about quantization.

It is the single technique that turns a 1.6 terabyte download into something that fits on a desk.

But first - what the heck is quantization anyway?

What Quantization Actually Does

Every model is a giant collection of numbers called weights. At training time each weight is usually stored in 16-bit or 32-bit floating point.

Quantization stores those same weights with fewer bits. Fewer bits per weight means less memory, less data to move per token, and therefore faster generation on bandwidth-bound hardware like Apple Silicon.

The price you pay is precision.

Push the bit count too low and the model starts to forget facts, lose track of long instructions, and make sloppy tool calls.

The memory math is one line:

Memory (GB) ≈ Parameters (billions) × Bits per weight ÷ 8

Add roughly 10 to 30 percent on top for the KV cache, runtime buffers and the operating system.

A 70-billion-parameter model at 4.5 bits per weight needs about 39 GB for weights alone.

  • - 32 bits per weight, full single precision, used for training master weights and almost never for local inference.
  • - 16 bits, half precision, with a narrow exponent range that can overflow on large activations.
  • - 16 bits with FP32's exponent range and less mantissa precision; the default release format for most open models.
  • - 8-bit floats; E4M3 keeps more precision, E5M2 keeps more range. DeepSeek, Z.ai and Mistral now ship official FP8 checkpoints, so FP8 is effectively lossless reference quality for many 2026 models.

The New 4-Bit Floats: MXFP4 and NVFP4

  • - a microscaling 4-bit float from the Open Compute Project, where small blocks of 32 weights share one scale factor. Kimi K3 and Kimi K3.1 Pro ship natively in MXFP4 weights with MXFP8 activations, trained with quantization-aware training, which is why a 2.8-trillion-parameter model downloads at about 1.56 TB.
  • - NVIDIA's 4-bit float for Blackwell GPUs, with smaller 16-weight blocks and an FP8 scale for better accuracy. Mistral Large 4, Muse Spark Open, Inkling and Mistral Small 4 all ship NVFP4 checkpoints.

The key difference from older 4-bit schemes is quantization-aware training.

When a lab trains the model to live in 4 bits from the start, the quality loss largely disappears.

Integer Quantization: INT8 and INT4

  • - 8-bit integers with a scale per channel or per group; near-lossless for most models and widely supported on GPUs and CPUs.
  • - 4-bit integers, usually with a scale per group of 32 to 128 weights. This is the workhorse of local AI, and most GGUF, GPTQ and AWQ files are built on it.
  • - the first number is weight bits and the second is activation bits. W4A16 keeps activations in 16-bit for quality, while W4A4 squeezes both for maximum throughput on supported hardware.

GGUF Legacy Quants and K-Quants

GGUF is the file format of llama.cpp, and by extension Ollama, LM Studio and Jan. Its quant names look cryptic, but they follow a pattern.

  • - 8-bit, about 8.5 bits per weight, virtually indistinguishable from the original.
  • - the original "legacy" quants: one scale per block of 32 weights, simple and fast, but less accurate than the K-quants at the same size.
  • - about 6.6 bits per weight; the "I can't tell the difference" tier.
  • - about 5.7 bits per weight; an excellent quality-to-size trade-off for dense models.
  • - about 4.8 bits per weight; the default sweet spot for most local users.
  • - about 3.9 bits per weight; usable for large MoE models, noticeably weaker on small dense ones.
  • - roughly 2.6 to 3.4 bits per weight; an emergency option to squeeze a giant model into a smaller machine.

The "K" means super-blocks with nested scales, and the S, M and L suffixes mean small, medium and large. The M and L variants keep sensitive tensors such as attention and output layers at higher precision.

I-Quants and the Importance Matrix

  • I-quants (IQ4_XS, IQ3_XXS, IQ2_XXS, IQ1_S) - lattice-based codebook quants that pack more quality into fewer bits. IQ4_XS sits near 4.25 bits per weight, IQ3_XXS near 3.06, IQ2_XXS near 2.06, and IQ1_S near 1.56.
  • The importance matrix (imatrix) - a calibration pass that runs sample text through the model and records which weights matter most. Quants built with an imatrix protect those weights, and below 4 bits the imatrix is the difference between usable and broken.

When you see "i1-GGUF" in a repository name, such as the mradermacher releases, that means imatrix-calibrated files.

Unsloth's Dynamic 2.0 quants (names like UD-Q4_K_XL or UD-IQ1_S) do not give every layer the same precision.

They keep critical layers at higher bit widths and crush the bulk of the MoE experts harder.

That is how Unsloth lists a 1-bit Mistral Large 4 at about 233 GB and a 1-bit Kimi K3 at about 594 GB, as reported in an M5 Ultra hosting guide.

Unsloth itself claims around 91 percent top-1 agreement for its smallest Mistral Large 4 quant, which is a vendor claim, so test it on your own prompts.

  • - post-training 4-bit quantization that uses second-order information to minimise error, layer by layer; strong on NVIDIA GPUs via vLLM.
  • - activation-aware weight quantization, which protects the small fraction of weights that see the largest activations; fast and popular for vLLM and SGLang serving.
  • - ExLlama's formats with fractional bit rates such as 4.65 bpw, letting you fill a GPU to the last gigabyte.
  • - half-quadratic quantization, which needs no calibration data and quantizes very quickly.
  • - the 4-bit NormalFloat format behind QLoRA fine-tuning, tuned for weights that follow a normal distribution.

MLX Quants for Apple Silicon

Apple's MLX framework has its own group-wise quantization at 3, 4, 6 and 8 bits, published under the mlx-community organisation on Hugging Face.

On Apple Silicon, MLX is often noticeably faster than llama.cpp for the same model.

One measured comparison on an M5 Ultra found DeepSeek V4 Flash at about 40 tokens per second under llama.cpp and about 53 tokens per second under MLX, according to an M5 Ultra benchmark.

That is roughly a third more speed from a software switch.

The KV cache stores the attention keys and values for every token in your context.

At a million tokens of context it can rival the weights in size.

Both llama.cpp and MLX can store the KV cache in 8-bit or 4-bit.

An 8-bit KV cache is nearly free in quality and halves context memory, while 4-bit is more aggressive and worth testing on long-document tasks first.

Architecture matters here too.

DeepSeek says V4.1 Flash cuts its KV cache to about a quarter of V4 Flash's, and hybrid linear-attention designs like Qwen's Gated DeltaNet and Kimi's Delta Attention shrink it further.

--------------  -----------------------  ----------------------  -------------------------  ---------------------------

Q5_K_M          5.7                      ~50 GB                  Very small                 Dense models, coding

Here is my rule of thumb.

Dense models below 40B: stay at Q5_K_M or higher.

Mid-size MoE models: Q4_K_M or MLX 4-bit.

Trillion-parameter MoE models: whatever fits, because a 2-bit giant often beats an 8-bit dwarf.

Choosing the Memory Sizes

Why 2,048 GB for enterprises?

Why a 64 GB floor for power users?

These numbers are not arbitrary.

They come straight out of the file sizes of the models that matter in late 2026.

Why 2,048 GB for the Enterprise Cluster

The new open frontier is enormous.

Kimi K3.1 Pro is a 2.8-trillion-parameter model that downloads at about 1.56 TB in its native MXFP4 format, as confirmed in a Kimi K3.1 Pro weights report.

Mistral Large 4 is about 1,060 GB in official FP8, and Muse Spark Open needs about 1.63 TB in full BF16.

A single 512 GB Mac Studio cannot hold any of these at high precision.

Two machines (1,024 GB) hold some of them at 4-bit.

Four machines (2,048 GB) hold every one of them at its native or near-native precision, with room left over.

That headroom is not waste. It goes to three jobs:

  • - million-token contexts are now standard, and long agent sessions eat memory fast.
  • - every extra user or agent needs its own slice of cache.
  • - GLM-5.3 in FP8 (about 756 GB) and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash in FP8 (about 510 GB) fit side by side with more than 700 GB to spare, so a coding model and a general model can both stay hot.

Four is also the natural size for a Thunderbolt 5 mesh.

Each Mac Studio can cable directly to the other three, so every node is one hop from every other node, and there is no switch to buy or fail.

That mesh is fast because of RDMA.

Apple added RDMA over Thunderbolt 5 in macOS 26.2, and Jeff Geerling's cluster test showed exo with RDMA speeding up as nodes were added while llama.cpp over TCP slowed down.

On Qwen3 235B, exo went from 19.5 tokens per second on one node to 31.9 on four, according to AppleInsider's write-up.

With the 2026 M5 Ultra, each node brings 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth.

Four of them reach about 4.8 TB/s in aggregate, a figure exo Labs highlights in its four Mac cluster announcement.

Why 512 GB nodes rather than eight 256 GB nodes?

TechRepublic notes that two 256 GB Mac Studios cost about $700 less than one 512 GB machine, so smaller nodes are cheaper per gigabyte.

But eight nodes cannot form a direct mesh, every extra hop adds synchronisation latency, and every extra box adds cables, power bricks and failure points.

Four big nodes is the sweet spot.

Why a 64 GB Floor for Power Users

The 2026 mid-size models are astonishingly good.

Qwen3.8-27B posts 61.7 on SWE-bench Pro, and its 4-bit build is only about 17 GB, according to a Qwen3.8-27B analysis.

So why not 24 GB or 32 GB?

Because the floor is about running the best small models , not just running them.

  • At 64 GB, Qwen3.8-27B or Gemma 4 31B runs at near-lossless 8-bit (around 29 to 33 GB of weights), with room for a long context window and your IDE, browser and agent tools.
  • At 64 GB, every MoE model up to the 35B class runs at 8-bit, and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt runs with an enormous context budget.
  • At 128 GB, you add the 100B-class MoE models: gpt-oss-120b (about 65 GB native), Mistral Small 4 and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B at 4-bit.
  • At 256 GB, you add DeepSeek V4 Flash at 4-bit (about 151 to 162 GB).

Frontier Research at Scale: Why I Chose 2 TB for 100-Agent Teams

The Millennium Prize Problems.

Fault-tolerant quantum computing.

These are the problems I care about most, and they are exactly where cloud AI pricing breaks down.

This section explains why I chose a 2 TB unified memory setup, and why the reason is not chat - it is coordinated teams of 100 or more agents.

What Frontier Research Actually Consumes

Research on open problems is not one clever prompt.

It is thousands of attempts, most of them failures, each re-reading long contexts full of definitions, prior attempts and formal proof states.

  • Attempt counts are enormous. For its best ARC-AGI score, OpenAI's o3 in high-compute mode needed 1,024 attempts per task, and the Arc Prize Foundation later revised its cost estimate from about $3,000 to as much as $30,000 per task, as TechCrunch reported.
  • A single benchmark run can reach seven figures. Simon Willison's back-of-envelope estimate for o3's high-compute run on the 400 public ARC-AGI puzzles came to roughly $1.15 million.
  • Real open problems do fall to agents - the easier ones. An agent that alternates LLM generation with Lean verification resolved 9 of 353 open Erdős problems at a per-problem cost of a few hundred dollars, according to an arXiv proof-search paper. Problems at the level of P vs NP are a different order of difficulty, and nobody - human or machine - knows what a solution will cost.
  • Even big companies hit the wall. CodingScape reports that Uber exhausted its 2026 AI budget in four months, in its open-weight LLM guide.

The Autumn AI Took On the Millennium Problems

When I first wrote this section, I said no AI system had solved a Millennium Prize Problem.

Here is what happened in the autumn of 2026.

Read the dates carefully, because every claim below is still waiting on human review.

  • Navier-Stokes with a smooth force (8 September). OpenAI announced that about 10,000 autonomous agents on an unreleased internal model had found a finite-time blow-up in the Navier-Stokes equations, as Quanta Magazine reported. Forcing is allowed in the official Clay statement, but the result arrived with a public credit dispute involving NYU's Tristan Buckmaster and Anthropic's Levent Alpöge, per Science News.
  • Navier-Stokes with no outside force (20 November). Buckmaster and Alpöge posted a 79-page paper claiming blow-up for the unforced 3D equations, the version many mathematicians regard as the real problem, per AI Weekly's alert. It comes with a Lean formalisation of about 600,000 lines, but the certificate it relies on had not been released and the paper is not peer reviewed, per FourWeekMBA.
  • The Riemann Hypothesis (20 November). Alpöge announced a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, and of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions, found with Claude over about six weeks and released as a Lean proof of roughly 17 million lines. Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative certified the formal proof on 21 November, per The Rundown, while the human-readable explanation is still a working draft and mathematicians are still working through what the proof does, per Crypto Briefing.
  • VP versus VNP (23 November). Anthropic posted a 70-page paper, with Claude as the sole author, claiming that Valiant's 1979 conjecture holds over every field, with a Lean formalisation of 324 files and 72,932 lines, per Pasquale Pillitteri's report. The README says no human mathematician has checked it, and the paper says it does not settle P vs NP, per FourWeekMBA's brief.

The Riemann result had a quieter prelude.

In August, a research version of Claude raised the proven share of zeta zeros on the critical line from 41.6 percent to 67.2 percent, per Anthropic's zeta note - real progress, but not a proof.

So where does the scoreboard stand?

Is 100 agents realistic on four Mac Studios?

Yes, with one honest caveat.

Research agents spend much of their time waiting on tools - Lean proof checks, Python experiments, quantum simulators, literature search - so far fewer than 100 are generating tokens at any instant.

The fast, small-active workers (8B to 16B active for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, 6B for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next) carry the volume, and the heavy reasoners are called only when a decision needs them.

Agent swarms at this scale are already real.

How the Agents Coordinate

A team of 100 agents without structure is just 100 expensive random walks.

The coordination layer is what turns a swarm into a research group.

  1. breaks the problem into sub-goals - lemmas, special cases, reductions, counterexample hunts - and assigns them.
  2. stores every definition, partial result, failed approach and open question, so no agent repeats a dead end.
  3. work in parallel: literature review, conjecture generation, proof search in Lean 4, counterexample search in code, and numerical experiments.
  4. treat the Lean kernel as ground truth. A proof that does not compile is not a proof, which is the same principle behind the Erdős results above.
  5. attack every claimed result before it reaches the blackboard as "established".
  6. writes everything up for the human researchers who decide what matters.

Quantum research has its own memory hunger.

A full state-vector simulation stores 2ⁿ complex amplitudes at 16 bytes each:

Memory (bytes) = 16 × 2ⁿ        where n = number of qubits
  • 35 qubits need 512 GB, which fills one Mac Studio node.

So a single 512 GB node can hold a 34-qubit state vector with room to spare, while the agent team searches error-correcting codes, circuit compilations and variational ansätze around it.

Tensor-network and stabilizer simulators go much further for structured circuits, and the same agents can write and run them.

Will a 100-agent team on four Mac Studios settle P vs NP?

You would need 10,000+ to 100,000+ agents for that. Maybe even 1 million agents.

AI sovereignty means you, your company or your country can keep using AI on your own terms, no matter what a vendor, a regulator abroad or a supply shock decides.

Owning the weights and the hardware is the most direct way to get there.

It is also the only way to ensure your company is running irrespective of internet outages, natural disasters, international calamities or war.

  • Models change under you in the cloud. On 14 September 2026, DeepSeek began routing every request for V4-Pro to V4.1 Flash at Flash prices, per DeepSeek's V4.1 announcement. A good change for most users - but not one they chose.
  • Prices and caps change under you. Cloud providers tune quotas, prices and acceptable-use policies continually, and your workflows inherit every change.
  • Weights on disk do not change. The file you validated in November 2026 behaves identically in 2030.
  • Geopolitics touches everything. The open frontier is now led largely by Chinese labs, with Meta, Thinking Machines, NVIDIA, Google, OpenAI and Mistral supplying strong Western and European alternatives. A sovereign strategy keeps options from more than one jurisdiction.
  • obligations for general-purpose AI model providers applied from 2 August 2025, according to the Commission's GPAI guidelines. The open-source exemption is narrow, and DLA Piper's analysis notes that usage limits or supplementary licensing can disqualify a model, which matters for the many "modified MIT" licences above.
  • MeitY notified the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules on 13 November 2025 with phased commencement, including Rule 4 from 13 November 2026, per SCC Online's summary. Running inference in-house keeps personal data processing inside your own fiduciary controls.
  • GDPR, HIPAA and sector rules: local inference removes an entire category of cross-border transfer and third-party processor questions.

I am not a lawyer, and you should get legal advice for your jurisdiction.

But I strongly believe that every serious organisation should hold at least one capable model it controls completely.

  1. Pick at least two models from different labs and jurisdictions, for example GLM-5.3 and Mistral Large 4.
  2. Mirror the exact weight files internally, with checksums, so a takedown or a repository change cannot touch you.
  3. Pin the inference engine version that you validated.
  4. Keep a permissively licensed fallback, such as Inkling 2 Small (Apache 2.0) or DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (MIT).
  5. Review each licence's model-as-a-service clause before you expose a model to customers.

Local AI is the strongest privacy guarantee you can get - if you set it up properly.

A local model on a badly managed machine is just a new place for data to leak.

Architecture for Sensitive Workloads

  • put the inference cluster on its own VLAN, block outbound internet by default, and open egress only for scheduled, signed model updates. For the most sensitive work, run fully air-gapped.
  • keep embeddings, vector databases and source documents on the same isolated network, so retrieval never calls out.
  • FileVault on macOS, LUKS on Linux, and encrypted NAS volumes for document stores and model files.
  • single sign-on in front of Open WebUI or your API gateway, per-team model access, and role-based limits on which models can see which document collections.
  • log who asked what, which model answered, and which documents were retrieved, then protect those logs as carefully as the data itself.
  • decide how long prompts and outputs are kept, and purge them on schedule.

Why Uncensored Models Are Life Savers During Cyber Attacks

Ransomware is moving laterally through your network.

Your analyst pastes an obfuscated PowerShell loader into an AI assistant and asks what it does.

The AI assistant - refuses.

Safety-tuned models are trained to refuse requests that look like hacking.

The trouble is that defending against an attack looks exactly like studying one.

  • reports a 96.6 percent refusal rate on malicious cyber prompts, and Hugging Face says that is higher than other open-weight models it tested, per Magica's analysis.
  • clears 98.6 percent on the StrongREJECT refusal test.
  • received extra safety post-training because its weights are public.

Those are reasonable choices for public chatbots.

But in an incident room, a false refusal can cost you minutes, and minutes are what separate a contained incident from a company-wide outage.

At the same time, capability is clearly there.

GLM-5.3 scores 84.5 on CyberGym, a vulnerability-discovery benchmark, on its model card.

The knowledge exists inside these models; alignment decides whether your defenders can reach it.

What Defenders Actually Need from a Model

  • - explaining what a decompiled function or a suspicious script does, line by line.
  • - unpacking encoded PowerShell, JavaScript droppers and macro payloads so analysts can read them.
  • - reading firewall, EDR and authentication logs to reconstruct an attacker's path.
  • - writing YARA rules, Sigma rules and SIEM queries for the exact sample in front of you.
  • - dissecting lures, headers and credential-harvesting pages.
  • - generating hypotheses about where an attacker might go next.
  • Authorised red-team simulation - rehearsing attacker behaviour inside a written scope, so the blue team can practise.
  • - turning chaotic notes into clear timelines for executives and regulators.

An uncensored local model does all of this without arguing, without sending your malware samples or breach details to a third party, and without a rate limit in the middle of the night.

During a breach, you may not be able to trust your own network, your SaaS accounts or your internet connection.

A model running on an isolated Mac Studio or a disconnected workstation keeps working when everything else is suspect.

And sending live incident data to an external API during a breach is a disclosure decision your legal team should make deliberately - not something an analyst should do at 3 a.m. by accident.

Governance: Power with Guard Rails

Uncensored models are powerful tools, so treat them like any other powerful tool.

  • to named security staff.

  • on a dedicated analysis network with no route to production.

  • Log every prompt and response for later review.

  • Write an acceptable-use policy that covers defensive work, authorised testing scope and prohibited uses.

  • Keep an aligned model for everyone else. The uncensored model belongs in the security toolkit, not on every desk.

  • Vet the abliterated build using the provenance checklist above.

The community already publishes hundreds of abliterated models, browsable in catalogues such as Featherless's abliterated catalogue, including some aimed at security work, but you must test any such model yourself.

Good news - the defenders now have frontier-grade help that never says no.

Bad news - so do the attackers, which is exactly why your team cannot afford to work with one hand tied behind its back.

Reprise: The Honest Case Against Going Local

You just told me a 128 GB box will never pay for itself if I only use Qwen3.8-27B lightly.

You told me a four-node cluster generates Kimi K3.1 Pro at the speed of a fast typist.

Cloud APIs for open models are cheap, they scale instantly, and someone else patches the servers.

With Cloud APIs, I do not need to pay for upgrades and maintenance.

2 TB is overkill for most small businesses.

All true and agreed to. But -

But cost per token was never the whole story.

You cannot rent sovereignty, you cannot rent an air gap, and you cannot rent a model that will help you dissect ransomware at 3 a.m. without logging your breach on someone else's server.

And the curve only bends one way.

The same kind of four-Mac Studio cluster that ran Kimi K2 Thinking in late 2025 runs far more capable models today, because the models keep getting more efficient while the hardware you already own stays paid for.

The smart move is hybrid.

Run the private, sensitive, high-volume and always-on work locally, and keep a cloud API for the rare task that needs the biggest closed model.

  1. Will the cloud API survive a war in your country?

  2. If the AI bubble pops, where will you get your AI?

  3. If all leading AI labs increase costs to cover their bills, what will you do with your current budget?

  5. If you need complete privacy, how can you trust a Chinese company’s APIs?

  6. If your company is banned by mistake, what will you do?

  7. If your infrastructure goes down, and you are running a mission-critical business, where is your backup?

  1. If one of your systems are hacked, how will you fight back? Will you feed sensitive company data into foreign servers?

  2. If your system requires cyberattack analysis, how will you bypass safeguards on US AI Companies?
